The outcomes and analysis presented here can serve as a foundation for further research in time series forecasting and neural network modeling. This paper examines the properties of homogeneous Zinbiel algebras, revealing in the process that all such algebras are inherently abelian. Furthermore, the paper establishes a link between N-derivative algebras and multilinear algebras, specifically in the context of homogeneous Zinbiel algebras, leading to the creation of two new categories, homogeneous Zinbiel multilinear spaces and homogeneous N-multilinear spaces. The paper's findings culminate in the presentation of a homogeneous N-derivative algebra analogue to the famous Tetracovector Structure, offering implications for research in the field. The authors also provide a detailed list of homogeneous Zinbiel algebras of low dimensions, complemented by an invitation to explore the more general realm of low-dimensional N-derivative algebras. Lastly, the paper offers a first look at building new finite-dimensional non-simple N-derivative algebras over a field with a positive characteristic. The research presents a general construction method for such algebras and provides specific examples in the process. The paper concludes by opening the door to investigating the properties of N-derivative algebras over a ring comprising non-commuting elements. The authors suggest that further research in these areas would be a valuable contribution to the literature. The paper's work is accompanied by 11 figures illustrating the relationships between different types of multilinear structures. The research's findings were presented at the International Conference on Non-Associative Structures, held in Durban, South Africa. We analyze a 3-dimensional cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation with a potential for inverse square behavior, $V(x) = |x|^{-2} + |x|^2$, and develop a approach that separates the linear and nonlinear components to study its spectral and scattering properties. Utilizing this method, we examine the properties of the linear evolution operator and leverage this to investigate the behavior of solutions under certain conditions, specifically those where the energy remains bounded. As a result, we derive an expression for the coordinate representation of the scattering matrix. Additionally, we explore the behavior of soliton families born from the linear component and analyze their properties in the asymptotic regions of the scattering space. We also obtain explicit representations of the phase space amplitudes in both the soliton and scattering frameworks. Furthermore, we extend this method to investigate the properties of solutions starting from specific initial conditions. Notably, we find that solutions starting from the ground state of the linearized problem exhibit linear behavior, and similarly, solutions starting from specific minima of the potential exhibit linear behavior. Using this method, we derive explicit expressions for the linearized problem and the potential behavior of solutions. Our work provides a general approach to investigating the spectral and scattering properties of a wide range of nonlinear and inverse square potential problems. Notably, we derive a new expression for the short distance expansion of the two-particle scattering amplitude. Notably, this result reveals that the leading term is independent of the potential, and for certain cases, it can be computed analytically. We demonstrate the method's applicability to a range of problems, and in particular, we demonstrate its application to a 2-dimensional problem, and derive an expression for the short distance expansion of the 2-dimensional problem. We derive a new result for the long-distance expansion of the 2-dimensional problem as well. Notably, we find that the result reveals that the 2-dimensional problem is independent of specific details of the potential, and it can be computed analytically. Our work provides a new perspective on this class of problems, and it opens up possibilities for investigating a wide range of problems with similar behavior. We derive a new perspective on this class of problems, and it is relevant to a range of problems in random matrix theory. We examine an issue of migratory infectious disease spread, where host population divides into two segments: active hosts who move and can get infected, and dormant hosts who can't move but are immune to infection. Active hosts move freely and within the entire space while trying to escape from dormant hosts. In turn, dormant hosts adopt the strategy that minimizes the cost per active host caught. As a result, active hosts maintain a safe distance from dormant hosts. Assuming a standard infection model, we show that in the homogeneous scenario, a stable equilibrium exists. Furthermore, in the heterogeneous scenario with a finite population, we identify the precise distance maintained by active hosts from dormant hosts and establish conditions for disease spread. Finally, numerical simulations validate our analytical findings and reveal that population density and migration speed affect population dynamics. Additional analyses are also provided for non-symmetric host interactions and the effects of stochastic processes on population dynamics. All analytical results are corroborated by corresponding numerical simulations. The research is extended to investigate the effects of environmental factors, such as wind and population age, on host movement and population dynamics. In addition to analytical studies, we investigate disease spread in non-linear media using mathematical transform techniques and establish a connection with the stand-and-wait issue. The research is also applied to investigate population dynamics in games with repeated interactions and complementarity of interactions. Lastly, we research the effects of population dynamics and disease spread under the constraints of environmental factors such as wind and population division into two segments: flying and non-flying hosts with different flying speeds and vision capabilities. As a result, flying hosts maintain a safe distance from the vision range of non-flying hosts. Using the established models, we investigate the effects of population division and flying speeds on population dynamics and show through numerical simulations that population division and flying speeds affect population dynamics. The majority of these exoplanets are detected through automated surveys, resulting in a large pool of discovered transiting exoplanets exceeding 4000 to date. The diversity of these exoplanets spans a broad spectrum, including various orbital periods, sizes, and planetary masses, making them ideal subjects for studying both the host planets and the underlying celestial physics. The results revealed a significant role for tidal interactions in shaping the K2-138 system, with planets b and c experiencing the greatest impact. However, models failed to account for the observed resonance sequence without including additional effects such as viscous dissipation in the inner planets. Notably, incorporating such viscous dissipation increased the orbital period of inner planets, aligning with expectations based on numerical simulations of protoplanetary disk dynamics. To maintain water's unique properties, it is crucial that hydrogen bonds associate and dissociate quickly.  Liquid ice, despite being disordered, contains small areas of hydrogen-bonded structures that ensure bond formation and dissolution occur rapidly.  These microstructures, however, are yet to be directly observed in water.  By utilizing neutron spectroscopy, it has been discovered that supercooled water and ice contain distinct structures that accommodate hydrogen bonds associating and dissociating at various rates.  Notably, hexagonal ice contains small areas where hydrogen bonds can develop slowly, which could be a reason water doesn't easily turn into these structures at lower temperatures.  This discovery also provides insight into how liquid water maintains its unique characteristics and why certain hydrogen-bonded structures become unstable in water.  Furthermore, this finding raises the possibility that certain defects in ice, previously thought to contribute to its unique properties, may actually play a different role than initially understood.  Specifically, it is suggested that certain water defects in hexagonal ice, previously believed to contribute to its slow association and dissociation rates, may actually do the opposite. The verification of theorems and formal proofs is a well-established practice.
However, the majority of the tasks involved are still performed manually, with
much of the effort concentrated in the initial stages of the process. To
rectify this, our research aims to develop more effective methods for the
creation and maintenance of formal proofs by analyzing the structure of Isabelle formal proofs through graph representations and associated techniques. 
Our proposed approach has been demonstrated through a case study on the Archive of Formal Proofs, showing how the introduction of a framework can facilitate the identification of problems within proof structures, highlight areas of strength or weakness within proof contributions, and track proof-related changes and developments. 
Ultimately, the ultimate goal is to utilize this framework as a platform for enhancing contributions to the Archive of Formal Proofs and fostering more productive interactions among the community of formal proof developers. 
In addition, we plan to further develop this platform as a comprehensive proof-basin for learning and teaching formal proof development and verification methods. 
Ultimately, the platform can be utilized as a collaborative tool for the Isabelle community and formal proof developers at large. 
Our platform is available at https://isabelleframework.org. 
A corresponding video illustrating the platform's functionality can be accessed at https://youtu.be/8u3bttl6g3Y. 
A comprehensive report detailing our findings is accessible at https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-03411145. 
Our source code, including the Isabelle framework and the associated Python code, is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/leobass/IsabelleFramework. 
By replicating the code and leveraging our platforms, our research can serve as a starting point for future development and community collaboration. 
In particular, the community can replicate the platforms themselves, as well as teach and learn from them. 
Ultimately, our research can contribute to a more unified and cohesive environment for the Isabelle community and formal proof developers. 
One key aspect of the platform's design is its modular structure, with each module replicable and easily understandable.

This paper introduces an exact two-stage robust optimization method to solve problems with uncertain constraints at known points. The objective is to complete a task with optimal results while considering various possible scenarios for the parameters. The traditional approach for such problems involves assuming a bounded range for the parameters, but this can lead to incomplete solutions if the true values are not within this range. In contrast, this method provides exact solutions for any given parameter values without the need for strict bounding. The method is based on a Lagrangian dual decomposition and utilizes a multiplier to account for uncertainty. An efficient solution strategy is developed to compute multipliers and verify optimality, and numerical results demonstrate its effectiveness for problems with up to 20 variables and hundreds of scenarios. The method is particularly valuable for its scalability and ability to handle complex problems that cannot be solved using other approaches. Finally, an extension of the method is introduced to handle more complex constraints with uncertain values. The results demonstrate its potential to solve real-world applications such as the capacitated vehicle routing problem with uncertain demands. The method is able to solve large instances of this problem that are beyond the capabilities of other approaches. A semi-transitive orienting of a graph $G$ implies that following a specific direction, any higher-induced subgraph retains a similar direction. This study investigates various properties of semi-transitive graphs. Specifically, we examine the threshold for semi-transitivity in split graphs of order $n$, identifying it as $n/2$. Additionally, we categorize semi-transitive split graphs, revealing that semi-transitivity within these graphs is either ubiquitous or confined to specific subgraphs of arbitrary size. Moreover, we establish the non-determinism complexity of checking semi-transitivity in split graphs, classifying it as $\mathcal{NP}$-complete for all cases except $n\geq 5$. Lastly, we explore the maximum number of semi-transitive orientations in split graphs, deriving an $n$-dependent upper limit for this value. However, we find this limit insufficient for $n\geq 5$ and propose an alternative, lower limit in relation to the number of induced subgraph sizes present in the graph. Specifically, for $n\geq 5$, we have established a lower semi-transitivity limit of $\lfloor n/3\rfloor$. This study further investigates this issue and provides supporting examples, illustrations, and pseudo-code for its results. The proposed research indicates that semi-transitivity is generally a less restrictive property than reversibility, and semi-transitivity is more easily characterized in graphs of order $n$ via more lenient conditions such as $\lfloor n/3\rfloor$ versus $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$. The transmission loss in photonic crystal fibers is attributed to the Brillouin scattering process, which can lead to both longitudinal and lateral interactions between neighboring modes. Through numerical modeling and finite element analysis, we have found that the transfer of heat-induced strain between modes is possible even when they lack mechanical coupling. This implies that the spread of heat along the fiber is not confined to paired modes and can lead to broader loss spectra. As the number of heat-induced modes increases, the corresponding loss spectrum becomes more widespread, suggesting that the loss could be directed toward specific modes and potentially utilized in applications such as mode multiplexing and spatially encoded sensing. Furthermore, we have identified a method to control the direction of loss by introducing mechanical coupling between the modes through tapers of varying geometry. This ability to manipulate loss and heat transport makes photonic crystal fiber platforms attractive for applications in optics and related fields. This research provides a framework for understanding and controlling the spread of heat and loss in photonic crystal fibers and related structures. To enhance safety and automated driving, accurately assessing human mobility risks is vital.
The primary obstacle hindering the development of automated vehicles is often identified as being involved in high-risk interactions with vulnerable road users, in particular cyclists.
Existing approaches for evaluating cyclist behavior primarily rely on inertial sensors, either as standalone technology or combined with cameras, which are subject to interferences and limitations in urban environments.
A novel video-based method for automatically detecting and mitigating the risks of cyclist collisions on the roads has been developed, focusing initially on capturing the three key motion characteristics of a cyclist's movement.
The proposed approach incorporates contextual information and is designed to be adaptable to diverse cycling styles.
The inherent complexity of the problem necessitates the development of a more sophisticated and balanced dataset of cyclist behavior to inform advanced automated driving systems.
The success of this approach is demonstrated through experimental results on real-world journeys, which showcase its potential for informed decision-making in automated vehicles. 
Ultimately, the aim is to leverage this technology to inform and optimize vehicle autonomy systems for increased safety on the roads.

Future traffic predictions are crucial for improving the efficiency of the road network. Most existing approaches have made significant advancements in predicting traffic speed or flow by using various features, however, they often overlook the importance of dynamic motion patterns. As shown in our study, these patterns substantially contribute to enhancing predictive performance. To address this limitation, we propose a novel model called MoDeRNN that integrates a novel block named MoDeBlock consisting of 3 directions of attention to capture motion details in all directions. MoDeBlock is further divided into 3 parts: encoding, decoding, and matching to represent motion details in varied phases. The matching block uniquely captures motion patterns between road segments. By incorporating MoDeBlock into RNN models, MoDeRNN achieves better performance compared to baseline models, achieving up to a 9.21% improvement in metric MSE@10. When applied to OpenStreetMap road graphs, MoDeRNN demonstrates exceptional capability in spatial and temporal extension learning, achieving a metric NS@10 of 87.19%. This study explores the possibility of neutrinoless double electron positron emission in high-energy particle collisions, considering the case where the initial particles have a small mass and can be close to the top of the mass spectrum. A specific type of collision involving leptons is examined, and it's demonstrated that even a small deviation in the mass of these particles from their expected values can lead to a significant contribution to neutrinoless double beta decay. This effect arises from the interaction between different types of Majorana states, which have a high amplitude for occurring and interfere with one another. A particular type of collision involving leptons is most effective at producing the type of spectrum required for significant contribution to neutrinoless double beta decay. An estimate of the rate of this process is provided, and it's shown that it could be comparable to existing experimental limits under certain conditions. Furthermore, it's noted that this process could be detected using colliders with energies exceeding 100 TeV in the future. Finally, it's suggested that this process could serve as a means of directly testing the mass of the lepton, and specific constraints on its mass are derived based on existing experimental limits. This process could potentially be observed at the Future Circular Collider or even a hypothetical 100 TeV collider. The possibility of directly measuring the mass of the lepton at the Future Circular Collider is also discussed. The rate of this process is found to be on the order of $10^{49}$ per second when the mass of the lepton exceeds its expected mass by a certain amount, and it's shown that this rate can be significantly higher for specific types of collisions involving leptons. An upper bound on the mass of the lepton is derived based on existing experimental limits and it's found to be on the order of a few hundred thousand GeV. Importantly, it's noted that this rate can be significantly higher than existing experimental limits and it's within the reach of future colliders. Specifically, it's shown that this rate can be as high as $10^{49}$ per second at the Future Circular Collider. An appendix discusses the possibility of measuring Majorana nature using neutrinoless double electron positron emission in high-energy particle collisions. Studies have previously demonstrated the potential for significant contribution to neutrinoless double beta decay in high-energy particle collisions and a direct relationship between this process and neutrinoless double beta decay. This research focuses on understanding and analyzing the capacity of crystalline structures to withstand fractures. We explore both the theoretical underpinnings of this ability and its numerical framework, assessing how edge fractures impact the resilience of these materials. We establish that crystal edges exhibit increased resistance to fractures and that the effectiveness of this resistance varies based on the crystal's orientation. We demonstrate that crystal edges resist fractures in two primary ways, either by strengthening the bond at the edge or by redistributing stress through a network of complementary bonds. We show that the latter mechanism leads to a critical stress threshold beyond which the crystal can no longer withstand the applied stress. Our findings reveal that this critical threshold is directly related to the relative strength of the complementary bonds and can be calculated using the average and standard deviation of their distribution. We verify the accuracy of our theoretical model using simulations based on a realistic stress-diffusion process that mimics the behavior of real materials. While BERT excels at modeling bidirectional contexts through denoising autoencoding, its reliance on input masking overlooks positional dependencies, leading to inconsistent token representations. This paper presents XLNet, a more generalized pretraining approach based on autoregressive models that posits the presence of a hidden representation for each token. By avoiding input masking, XLNet captures positional dependencies explicitly and derives context from the presence of other tokens. Additionally, XLNet employs a permutational sampling strategy during pretraining, enabling the recovery of all possible permutations through permutations and contextualizations. As a result, XLNet often surpasses BERT on 20 out of 21 tasks, including aspects of the GLUE benchmark and the natural language inference dataset SNLI, further establishing its superiority. Moreover, XLNet achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MRPC and STS-B tasks, with performance improvements amounting to 14% and 3% respectively over BERT. Further experiments demonstrate XLNet's capability to handle out-of-vocabulary words during downstream tasks. While training XLNet necessitates significantly more samples and computations than BERT, optimizations through GPU and GPU+FPGA utilization mitigate these costs, enabling the use of XLNet effectively. Examples of XLNet's capabilities can be found at microsoft/xlnet. A comprehensive version of this work, including additional details and technical aspects, is available online. The study of exoplanetary atmospheres via low-resolution transit spectroscopy has significant potential to uncover their properties; however, the influence of stellar activity is a major concern for this approach. To assess its impact, we conducted a comprehensive study simulating transit spectroscopy of a hot Jupiter around an active star using synthetic data, factoring in variables like atmospheric scale heights and absorptions. To mitigate this effect, we also explored the advantages of utilizing high-resolution spectroscopy. The results showed that in cases where the absorptions are not strongly featured, stellar activity has a minimal impact on transit spectroscopy, whereas when absorptions are strong, activity can lead to false positives. To mitigate this effect, we found that knowing the ratio of chromospheric to photospheric flux, a measure of stellar activity, allows us to make informed decisions in scenarios where the absorptions are not strongly featured. Furthermore, we discovered that utilizing high-resolution spectroscopy can significantly improve our understanding of both the star and the exoplanet, providing valuable insights into the star's activity and potential atmospheric loss of the exoplanet. With the aid of synthetic data, we demonstrated that in cases where the absorptions are not strongly featured, stellar activity can be partially mitigated, whereas when absorptions are strong, more sophisticated methods such as high-resolution spectroscopy or multiple transit observations are required to uncover the planet's properties. The study concludes by suggesting that in scenarios where the absorptions are not strongly featured, stellar activity can be managed to some extent, whereas when absorptions are highly expressed, more advanced techniques are required. The study further concludes that utilizing high-resolution spectroscopy can provide valuable insights into the star and the exoplanet, providing a potential path forward for transit spectroscopy. The study provides a framework for understanding the impact of stellar activity and offers a potential solution to mitigate its effects. Galaxies that appear brightly in the infrared but relatively dimly in the optical are often associated with intense dust emission. Utilizing early data from JWST, we have identified a distinct group of these galaxies with extremely faint optical presence but robust infrared emission. Our research involves examining 12 such galaxies observed with NIRCam and MIRI instruments. Initial analysis with spectroscopic models indicates that the strong infrared emission in these galaxies can be attributed to a dense dust cloud containing young, hot stars, even though their optical emission is significantly obscured. Our findings also suggest that a large portion of their infrared radiation is generated through stochastic processes from young stars, rather than through active galactic nuclei power. These galaxies are predominantly compact and have low levels of star formation efficiency, which could be due to the presence of massive black holes regulating their activity. Our study indicates that the optical transparency of these galaxies is a result of interacting dust clouds rather than a widespread ionizing radiation field. Further investigation is required to fully grasp the nature and progression of these enigmatic galaxies. Based on their observed properties, we propose a classification system and present potential research paths for future follow-up studies. Our data and analysis are available online at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7014447. Our analysis suggests that these galaxies could be part of a broader family of dusty galaxies similar to Circumgalactic Envelope Dominated Galaxies, with further research needed to fully understand their development. We investigate the logic obtained by combining intuitionistic logic with the Wainwright logic, a hypersequent logic that allows for contraction. This logic is denoted as IHw. Our study focuses on the logic's properties after removing certain features that contribute to its complexity. Specifically, we examine the effect of alleviating the contraction rule in IHw, resulting in the logic IHA. Our analysis reveals that, in contrast to IHw, IHA has a decidability threshold for its modalities. Indeed, we demonstrate the decidability of several modal systems within IHA. Furthermore, we establish that, when certain rules are removed, the logic's modal system simplifies, becoming equivalent to a well-understood modal logic. For example, the modal version of IHA without the thickening rule mirrors the propositional tensor logic, a well-studied modal logic that is itself equivalent to S5. To further validate the notion that such modal logics are manageable, we show that both IHA without the right-hand side fusion rule and the modal version of IHA without the right-hand side fusion rule and thickening are each respectively decidably equivalent to and sublogics of the well-understood modal logic K. Additionally, we investigate the effect of other rule removals within IHw and IHw*, its equivalent modal version. Our study reveals that removing the left-hand side fusion rule yields a logic whose modal version mirrors that of non-classical hybrid logic. Similarly, the removal of the left and right-hand side fusion rules results in a logic whose modal version mirrors that of hybrid logic. Lastly, we examine the effect of removing the thickening rule, a rule known to contribute to complexity in certain logics. Our study shows that this rule is responsible for the complexity of IHw* but that its removal yields a logic with a relatively high degree of complexity. Despite this, our analysis shows that removing the right-hand side fusion rule results in a logic with a relatively low degree of complexity. Overall, our study provides a comprehensive evaluation of several rule removal methods within various hypersequent logics, providing valuable insights into the trade-offs between logical expressiveness and computational complexity. The study notably highlights the effectiveness of the right-hand side fusion rule removal strategy in achieving a balance between these two factors. We introduce a versatile model for elastic scattering that effectively accounts for significant dynamic effects, including ro-vibrational interactions, large amplitude zero-point effects, and significant coupling strength variations. This simplified phenomenological model is based on a fundamental Hamiltonian and establishes a direct link between measured parameters and physical concepts. Its utility is demonstrated in analyzing existing data and predicting outcomes for scattering systems yet to be studied. Examples encompass a range of systems involving diatomic molecules and hydrogen atom collisions. Although the model is primarily explored in the context of molecular beam scattering, its range of applications extends to other domains, including neutron scattering and optical second-harmonic generation. By providing explicit equations and algorithms for computing scattering observables using the Schrodinger multidimensional Newton-Raphson method, we open the possibility of a systematic approach to phenomenological elastic scattering studies, best suited for research environments. This approach offers a balance between simplicity and precision. Its results typically fall within 1% of highly accurate quantum mechanical calculations. Current techniques for site selection in multisite fMRI data analysis focus solely on maximizing t-values, which often results in overlooking the underlying data. In contrast, we introduce a new approach that utilizes statistical strength as a key factor in selecting reliable site pairs. Our results show that using statistical strength leads to the selection of a majority of strong, highly reliable connections (over 70%), which in turn yields more precise predictions compared to the conventional method based on t-values. Additionally, we found that using statistical strength enables the detection of weak, highly reliable connections (which are typically overlooked by the conventional approach) and ultimately results in more accurate predictions. In fact, our predictions show improved precision in both strong and weak connections. Overall, our findings suggest that using statistical strength as a criterion for selecting reliable site pairs improves our understanding of neural networks and leads to more precise predictions of connectivity. These predictions, in turn, can help shed light on the complex relationships within large brain networks. Ultimately, our research aims to lay the groundwork for developing precision-oriented algorithms that identify reliable site pairs for analysis. Such algorithms may lead to significant breakthroughs in neuroscience and machine learning fields. To verify our results and compare the two approaches, we conducted an extensive analysis of a comprehensive dataset consisting of 15 public resting-state fMRI datasets across 312 site pairs. Our results demonstrate that using statistical strength as an analysis criterion yields highly reliable connections (top 70%), which in turn result in more precise predictions of functional neural connections. These predictions, in turn, show improved spatial consistency and temporal stability. In contrast, the conventional approach based on t-values identifies only a smaller subset of highly reliable connections (around 30%). These findings indicate that using statistical strength as an analysis criterion improves our understanding of weak, highly reliable connections, which in turn result in more precise predictions of functional neural connections. Our results also show that the predictions made using statistical strength as an analysis criterion exhibit improved spatial consistency and temporal stability. The widespread adoption of large-N radio interferometers is hindered by their substantial computational requirements for data processing and analysis. Among the various processing techniques employed, traditional gridding remains one of the most common methods of recovering visibility data despite its high computational costs. In an effort to mitigate these expenses, researchers have developed methods such as Chirp Corrected Imaging and Fast Imaging, which can process and image data in a more efficient manner by first reducing the complexity of the input data and then distributing it across multiple cores for optimization. This research aims to develop an improved, scalable gridding method for efficient computation of underdetermined radio interferometer data. By leveraging the properties of regular grid constructions, we develop a new method that can take advantage of existing optimization techniques like FFT to process the data in a more time-efficient manner. This approach also allows us to analyze its computational complexity and compare its performance with other state-of-the-art methods like Fast Imaging for practical applications. Through numerical simulations, we evaluate the various processing methods in terms of their computational efficiency for sparse, regularly arranged antennas and find that our proposed method outperforms others with a more linear scaling of computational complexity. Additionally, we demonstrate that our method is compatible with the most common visibility weighting schemes and consider methods for optimizing the direction of the gridding vectors to further improve its efficiency. This research provides a foundation for the development of more efficient algorithms in this domain and is expected to have a significant impact on the practical applications of radio interferometer data processing. Ultimately, we hope that our findings will contribute to the development of low-complexity, scalable methods for the processing of radio interferometer data. This paper introduces a new class of uniform spaces, known as standard spaces,
which can be viewed as a combination of the discrete topology and various
uniformities found in topological groups. We establish a framework for
ategorizing standard spaces, defining homeomorphisms, quasiconvex motions,
isometries, and left actions on these spaces. Furthermore, this work sets the
stage for a natural definition of group structures within this context, which
is explored further in a separate study. As a point of comparison, some
properties of topological groups are examined to see how they translate to the
world of standard spaces. Many of the concepts and results presented here
demonstrate a high degree of versatility and can be effectively applied to a
wide range of spaces, encompassing general metric spaces, manifolds, and
discrete sets, while also being inclusive of various types of spaces. This
research aims to lay the groundwork for a theory of group structures within the
context of standard spaces. Some notable results presented include a
definition of group structures within the context of standard spaces, which
requires quasiconvex motions to be compatible with the standard filter, and
proofs of the Bergman property, the Bogatycha distance theorem, and the
Riemannian geometry localization theorem for spaces with this new property. A
comprehensive list of open questions is also provided at the conclusion of this
work. We anticipate that the theorems and concepts presented here will be
useful not only for the existing theories of group structures and uniform spaces
but also for the emerging theory of group structures within the context of
standard spaces. We envision that this theory of group structures within the
context of standard spaces will have far-reaching applications and may lead to
new insights and discoveries at the intersection of geometry, topology, and
group theory. As a result of our research, novel geometric and topological
properties of group structures within the context of standard spaces have been
identified, including a new property we call standard group, and associated
concepts such as standard group actions, for which we establish a definition
and demonstrate its potential to yield novel results. We also introduce the
concept of a group within the context of standard spaces, which requires
quasiconvex motions to be compatible with the standard filter, and prove the
group localization theorem for groups with this new property. We further
demonstrate that the set of motions on any group is a group

We explore how uncertainty associated with automatic speech recognition affects the task. Continual learning research focuses on developing new models that can handle multiple learning tasks without experiencing performance degradation or becoming stale on subsequent tasks. Pre-trained models, particularly those trained on large unsupervised datasets like language models, are seen as an attractive solution to this challenge. However, it's unclear whether these models are truly beneficial in continual learning applications, and if so, what benefits they provide. This paper investigates this question by examining the potential value of utilizing pre-trained models in continual learning. To do this, we examine how pre-trained language models, such as BERT and GPT-2, perform when used in a basic continual learning setting, and compare their results to a more straightforward approach that fine-tunes individual models for each task. Our study reveals that these models are not necessarily providing added value in continual learning scenarios, and that the simpler method often outperforms or matches the performance of the pre-trained models. As a result, accurately detecting hate speech has become crucial, and essential for maintaining social cohesion. To advance research in this field, we propose an understandable hate speech identification system that not only pinpoints toxic content but also enables users to comprehend its breakdown. A major obstacle in hate speech identification is accurately pinpointing its core components, particularly given the unstandardized nature of linguistic features and the lack of clear definitions surrounding hate speech-related terms. To overcome this challenge, we suggest a dual neural network approach for identifying hate speech and extracting key features. A major challenge in explaining AI-based decisions lies in bridging the gap between human and machine understanding. We tackle this issue by leveraging the inherent transparency of word-level rationalizations. A thorough examination of our system reveals that its primary factors contributing to hate speech include derogatory language, agitation, and reference to social group identities. We initially present a comprehensive dataset of hate speech-related toxic content, and provide a detailed analysis of its characteristics. The methodology successfully characterizes and reduces the dimensionality of this medical imaging data, enabling accurate diagnosis of brain diseases to be achieved via the GIFC capability region. Neural network-based models have become ubiquitous in various applications. Their large size, however, can hinder deployment in resource-constrained environments. Research has recently been directed towards compressing these models, specifically through reducing the number of parameters in pre-trained models. Unlike other approaches focused on modifying the loss or output predictions, InDistill proposes an approach based on knowledge distillation that preserves data flow. This results in the compressed model producing the same output as the original model when given the same input data. This data-preserving property enables InDistill to be used in conjunction with existing loss functions. InDistill utilizes feature features extracted from the original model due to their inherent interpretability. As such, it is compatible with models featuring skip connections, residual bridges, and layer-normalization. InDistill offers several benefits, including improved model compression accuracy and reduced memory requirements without sacrificing accuracy. This approach also enables the compressed model to be more resilient to quantization errors. Our experiments demonstrate InDistill to be effective on a range of tasks, including image classification on CIFAR and ImageNet, and speech recognition on TIMIT. InDistill, however, may not yield comparable results for models lacking distinct feature features, specifically those involving spatial attention mechanisms. This limitation is also a characteristic of existing distillation-based approaches. Overall, InDistill offers a novel and efficient compression strategy, effectively extending the applicability of knowledge distillation in data-preserving model compression. Although it may not be universally applicable, it represents a highly competitive approach, especially for models featuring interpretable feature features. Implementation is available on GitHub under the open-source repository distill-cifar. This code has been actively maintained and updated since its initial release in 2019. InDistill has also been made available as part of the Open Source Model Compression Library under the terms of the MIT License agreement. Models compressed using InDistill have been deployed in various embedded systems due to their exceptional performance, specifically those supporting the NCS2 PYNQ platform, an embedded development suite. This paper introduces a frequency-based parent selection approach to mitigate the negative consequences of asynchronous evaluation times. Our proposed solution involves grouping individuals according to their generation and using a parent selection mechanism that favors older, high-fitness generations. Our research demonstrates that, compared to a conventional parent selection method, the frequency-based approach yields superior results across three test functions: 1) faster convergence, 2) higher precision, and 3) greater diversity. However, when applied to more complex PDEs, it often experiences a problem known as spectral bias. One way to improve PINN's performance is by using a heavier momentum technique during training. By doing so, it appears that increased momentum reduces spectral bias. Our research focuses on the Cosmic Ray Albedo Neutron Decay (CRAND) source, evaluating its impact on the neutrons produced near the surface of Earth. We're particularly interested in how these neutrons contribute to the detection of high-energy cosmic rays. We've developed a Monte Carlo simulation to analyze this process, breaking it down into three stages: cosmic-ray proton incidence, neutron production, and in-flight decay. Using this simulation, we've determined the proportion of cosmic rays originating from CRAND sourced particles, with a significant majority (56.9% at 10-11 GeV) to 63.2% (at 100-111 GeV) coming from this local source. We've observed that the CRAND signal enhances the flux of cosmic rays at lower energy thresholds, with a more noticeable effect at 10-20 GeV. We've also identified a way to distinguish CRAND signal particles from regular cosmic rays through their varying production depths, with a potential significant impact (up to two times more particles) at detecting CRAND signal at very high energy thresholds (above 100 GeV). Our research suggests that the CRAND source is a crucial factor for understanding the production of cosmic rays. A massive planet may be forming around CIDA 1, a very low-mass star located in the Rho Ophiuchi star-forming region. By analyzing near-infrared images and spectra, researchers discovered that the light coming from this star is being scattered by dust grains. Since CIDA 1 is not producing much dust, it is likely that the grains are being shaped into particles by the pressure of the wind coming from the star. By modeling this effect, scientists found that there needs to be a massive planet, weighing at least 10 times the mass of Jupiter, located at a distance of about 0.2 astronomical units from the star. This planet may be responsible for creating a wind gap and altering the pressure and density of the gas and dust in the disk, causing small grains to form. Alternatively, it is possible that the dust is being shaped by the fragmentation of ice droplets that are being splashed by the star's rosette rings, a phenomenon that occurs when ice droplets are hit by X-rays coming from a nearby active star. However, further observations are needed to confirm the presence of this massive planet and study the conditions in the disk surrounding CIDA 1. In the future, researchers may be able to detect this massive planet directly by observing the star using advanced telescopes, such as the Giant Magellan Telescope or the European Extremely Large Telescope, which will be able to detect the star's light being scattered by dust grains or use alternative methods to detect the planet. By studying this massive planet and the disk surrounding CIDA 1, researchers will be able to gain a better understanding of the process of planet formation and migration, which will help in understanding the conditions that form and shape the planets in our solar system and other similar systems. Review-based product recommendation is a crucial component of e-commerce, allowing users to rely on the opinions of others to make informed purchasing decisions. Prior studies primarily focused on understanding the content and context of reviews, neglecting the user's sentiment. This paper proposes a novel framework, Sentiment-sensitive Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN), to model reviews interactively with user features, incorporating both the writer's sentiment and content. By utilizing a more comprehensive review feature space, SIFN outperforms comparative methods in various product recommendation tasks. Additionally, the study demonstrates the effectiveness of interactive modeling in recommendation systems. Notably, SIFN has been successfully applied in a real-world setting at Meituan Dianping, a leading Chinese mobile e-commerce platform, enhancing user experience. The research findings highlight recommendations with contrasting review counts and sentiment ratings, emphasizing the importance of interactive modeling and sentiment consideration in review-based product recommendation. Moreover, the study reveals that users often rely more heavily on positive reviews, while reviewers frequently provide more detailed information when leaving negative comments. Finally, the research shows that users tend to conflate review content and writer sentiment when making purchasing decisions. These insights offer valuable practical knowledge for developers to create more accurate and relevant product recommendations. Experimental evaluations and A/B testing on the Meituan Dianping platform validate these conclusions. The research also opens up potential avenues for further exploration, such as the impact of review content and writer sentiment on recommendation quality in different age groups and how users with varying levels of education rely on review-based recommendations. Ultimately, the study provides a deeper understanding of user behavior in online product recommendations. The research also identifies several potential challenges, such as the impact of cultural background on review content and writer sentiment. For example, users from Confucian cultures may place a higher premium on social harmony, making them more likely to write positive reviews. This study investigates the effectiveness of replacing single words with alternative options, mimicking natural substitutions found in code-switched datasets, in enhancing coding-switched models. Two distinct word substitution techniques are explored: (1) single-word substitution utilizing a language model; (2) pair-wise substitution combining code-switched words with monolingual options. Hexahedral meshes contain hexahedron elements that enable efficient computations. These meshes excel at accurately simulating various physical phenomena and their benefits are well-documented in the field of engineering simulations. However, hexahedral meshes are often constructed with difficulty due to limitations in current technology. To address this challenge, a new approach called untet is introduced, which simplifies the process of extracting hexahedral elements from pre-existing polygonal meshes. This untet algorithm can handle meshes with a wide range of tetrahedral element counts, from 4 to 58 percent hexahedral elements, while maintaining accurate hexahedral part estimations with an error rate of less than 4 percent. This innovation allows for the efficient construction of high-quality hexahedral meshes using the untet technique. Untet has been successfully applied to challenging meshes and has been used in the creation of several examples which demonstrate its capabilities, untet can for example be used to speed up simulations or improve the resolution of visualizations. Untet has been released under an open-source license allowing its widespread adoption in the field of computational geometry and mesh generation. Untet's source code can be accessed on github at https://github.com/andreabassi/untet. Current state-of-the-art systems for extracting relations from unstructured text are often limited by their reliance on pre-existing knowledge bases, which fail to account for relationships not previously documented. This paper explores an alternative approach, investigating whether tasks like link prediction can serve as a more comprehensive relation extraction method. To this end, a novel neural network architecture is proposed, designed to optimize the integration of both external knowledge bases and self-learned relation representations to improve performance. This system generates relation concepts in a common space as the existing knowledge base and unstructured text, bridging a potential gap in relation understanding. Experiments have demonstrated that this system is adept at recognizing relations in unstructured text, outperforming traditional systems based on pre-existing knowledge bases. Furthermore, results indicate that integrating link prediction tasks can enhance relation extraction capabilities, ultimately contributing to a more comprehensive and accurate relation understanding. Source code for this system is publicly available on GitHub. Overall, findings suggest that relation extraction can be viewed as a process of predicting links to complete knowledge graphs, rather than solely relying on pre-existing knowledge bases. This paper is an extension of a previously published conference paper at IJCAI 2020. Key differences between the two include the presentation of additional experimental results, updated code based on the Berzerk library, and the incorporation of supplementary material and code for berzerk.io. Recent research has highlighted the importance of limited fine-tuning in reinforcement learning (RL) to ensure low cognitive costs and robustness. We apply continuity concepts from metric geometry to RL, particularly to Markov decision processes (MDPs). Our findings show that even with only a 1/γ fraction of similar transitions in an RL state space metric (as defined by a subgeodesic distance) guarantee continuity. Moreover, in cases where optimal policies have a well-defined geometric structure (such as in linear or circular contexts), we demonstrate that the continuity fraction can be exponentially scaled. This new understanding of RL continuity sheds light on the trade-off between adaptability and computational efficiency, and highlights the need for coarsely-grained structure preservation in RL policies. Our results also lead to new open problems and questions, including the potential extension of our methods to more complex MDPs. Through a combination of behavioral tests and reverse-engineering the neural mechanisms from fMRI data, our findings reveal that the animacy structure comprises three integral components - a core inclusive of humans, animals, and humanoid faces, an extended section encompassing all animate entities, and a more loosely bound area encompassing all inanimate objects. This representation, rooted deeply within the ventral temporal cortex, appears to be an innate aspect of the visual system. When applied to other image categories like birds and insects, our model demonstrates remarkable generalizability. Moreover, our model can successfully decode complex animacy classifications in monkeys and humans, simply by observing their brain activity while viewing image pairs. To maintain the overall mass balance while calculating the average velocity in multidimensional simulations of incompressible fluid dynamics, researchers use mass-conserving methods such as superpenal and supersaturated filtering techniques. These methods, originally developed for one-dimensional and two-dimensional simulations, come with drawbacks like disrupting the solution arrangement and leading to over-correction when applied to three-dimensional simulations. This paper presents a new arrangement-preserving superpenal filtering method, compatible with higher-order elements, that ensures the solution's continuity and arrangement remains intact across all dimensions. This method employs a convex optimization approach to calculate the average velocity, and its effectiveness has been successfully demonstrated in diverse numerical simulation scenarios. Results show that the novel filtering technique achieves a significant 40% reduction in velocity perturbation compared to a previously established method, and its computational cost is approximately 10% higher. When compared to a non-arrangement-preserving method, the new technique achieves a 10-20% lower velocity perturbation while exhibiting a 10% increase in computational cost. Overall, the proposed optimization-based approach has been successfully applied and has shown substantial improvements in multidimensional simulations. Its potential extensions to other conservative quantities have also been explored. Additionally, the paper's findings have shed light on the generalization patterns of these quantities during smoothing operations. Further details on the research can be found in the accompanying demonstration note, included in the supplementary materials. Quasi-periodic fluctuations, specifically type-C QPFs, in the 1-50 keV range, have been observed in the MAXI J1535-571 data collected by the Insight-HXMT. A detailed analysis of these type-C QPFs reveals a correlation between their duration and flux, supporting the coronal oscillation model. Through phase lag calculations, it's determined that type-C QPFs delay the hard flux by approximately 0.02-0.04 s, suggesting that they cause vertical flow in the corona during the soft-to-hard phase. Observations indicate that the type-C QPFs in MAXI J1535-571 evolved from short to long periods over the course of its 780 s soft state interval. Furthermore, this evolution is linked to a decrease in count rates, implying that the type-C QPFs may have triggered a transition from the soft to hard state, marking a key development in corona evolution. A transition to the hard state was later reversed when type-C QPFs resumed their normal long-period behavior and the system entered a state characterized by delayed hard flux. Through detailed timing analyses, researchers have established a comprehensive understanding of MAXI J1535-571's corona development. By examining the type-C QPFs observed in Insight-HXMT data, researchers have gained valuable insights into the dynamics of black hole corona. Ultimately, this study paves the way for future investigations into the physical processes governing type-C QPFs and their role in shaping the dynamics of black hole corona. In multi-agent learning systems, intrinsic motivation plays a key role in initiating and sustaining learning processes. A new concept called transfer empowerment (TE) has been introduced as an intrinsic motivation mechanism that focuses on the agent's ability to discover solutions that are easily transferable to uncertain environments. From the social perspective, TE reveals properties that can be exploited by a social monitor to adjust the agent's motivation dynamically. Building on this discovery, a novel algorithm is developed to leverage TE's social model, enhancing motivation through a more nuanced understanding of the agent's learning dynamics in interaction with its partner. Through theoretical and empirical analyses, the intrinsic motivation mechanism demonstrated in this research exhibits consistent and predictable results that motivate consistent behavior in both theoretical and practical applications. Experimental findings further show that this mechanism is robust to varying conditions of social and environmental complexity and highlight TE's potential as a versatile learning framework for addressing diverse real-world challenges. Moreover, the mechanism's effectiveness is shown to be comparable to traditional methods of intrinsic motivation in promoting social cooperation and efficient learning outcomes. Key findings from these studies include the discovery of a measurable unit of TE that enables its quantification through observable agent behavior and the development of a social learning algorithm powered by TE's intrinsic motivation mechanism, which consistently yields cooperative and accurate solutions across multiple experiments. Overall, the research presents a novel framework for addressing and analyzing the complexities of motivation in social learning systems that are driven by transfer empowerment. Findings from this study are expected to contribute significantly to the ongoing research agenda in transfer empowerment and motivation research, which are rapidly evolving as key areas of interest in permissive, cooperative, and social learning. Substance identification, a critical function in fields including chemistry, forensic science, and cooking, involves determining the composition of an unknown material based on observable properties like its color, a task often beyond the capabilities of even the best AI models.  This study involves developing a simplified model to simulate substance interactions and using contrastive learning to identify substances from a variety of views.  By training the model on thousands of virtual substances, it is able to accurately identify substances in just one image after being introduced to a new substance for the very first time, a capability that no other approach has been able to achieve.  This achievement is further bolstered by the model's ability to generalize to substances that were not part of the original training dataset.  Moreover, the model's performance is superior to that of human chefs with extensive experience.  This study is the first to demonstrate successful one-shot substance identification across such a broad spectrum of views, a feat that opens up new possibilities for AI-powered substance identification and composition in a variety of settings.  This novel approach has the potential to significantly expand the range of applications for substance identification and composition. Traditional object detection methods rely on matching bounding box coordinates with class probabilities. However, this approach can be limiting as it relies heavily on accurate box coordinates. An alternative strategy involves directly matching image features with class probabilities, but this method has its drawbacks as historical detection data can't be easily utilized. Our proposed LoFTR method takes a different approach by bypassing the need for a detector all together. Instead, it locally matches distinct features in an image with a pre-defined class library stored in memory. An efficient transformer is used to compress and narrow down the field of possible matches, allowing a subsequent and more efficient comparison to identify the best match with reduced computational cost. Our experiments show that our method can effectively use pre-trained models to perform new detection tasks on different data sets with minimal or no fine tuning required. Additionally, our method has shown to be effective across a range of different data sets including images, point clouds and video frames. An analysis of our results has revealed that our method is able to accurately detect objects in 3D data with an mAP rate of 65% and also demonstrate a significant reduction in computational requirements when compared to other state of the art methods. In model compression, a large, complex model is approximated by a simpler one to reduce computational costs without performance losses. This study focuses on adapting traditional model compression, typically effective on fully observable problems, to partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs). We investigate whether previously effective compression methods can handle POMDPs, and specifically examine if observing a model's behavior through planning tasks enhances a model's susceptibility to compression. We find that using a model that has been trained but does not observe the planning task results in significantly better compression with smaller information-reduction ratios than methods originally effective on fully observable problems. This suggests that traditional model compression methods may achieve better results when a model's behavior is available, but may not adequately compress POMDP models. We therefore propose a new information-reduction method, leveraging a model that has been trained but does not observe the planning task to remove redundant information from POMDP models, achieving better compression with lower performance losses than the previous methods. Additionally, our proposed method allows for the flexibility to perform compression based on a model's behavior that has been trained but does not observe the planning task, and also enables the incorporation of a partial observability factor to improve the robustness of POMDP models to noise and information loss. We validate these results in experiments with POMDP tasks, including to predict when to use a surgical tool and plan for robot motion given limited sensory information. We find our proposed method achieves up to 65% better compression with no performance losses, and reduces the total number of parameters in POMDP models by 80% with no performance losses and also ensures our proposed method achieves the same or better performance as it compresses fewer parameters. We establish novel $W^{1,p}$-estimates for measures defined on elliptic equations, where the diffusion matrix is irregular and potentially degenerate. This measures are restricted to the level set $\{u = 0\}$ of a function $u$, which satisfies a given elliptic equation. As a consequence of these estimates, we derive the interior and boundary $W^{1,p}$-regularity of the level set $\{u = 0\}$. Furthermore, under certain conditions on the diffusion matrix, we prove the $W^{1,1}$-differentiability of these surface measures. This differentiability is also proven for individual surfaces under specific conditions on the irregularities and the way they intersect. Our findings apply to a variety of problems in homogenization and periodic stochastic processes. Specifically, we investigate the behavior of periodic stochastic processes at various scales and confirm the known regularity of periodic surfaces, which was conjectured due to the nature of these processes. This research was inspired by the work of J. Bourgain on $W^{1,p}$-differentiability and applied to surface measures. Moreover, we extend the findings of P.-L. Lions in studying periodic stochastic processes and correct an error in his work regarding the level set $\{u = 0\}$, which he assumed to be $C^{0,1}$. This assumption is not necessary in our research. Finally, the work is further demonstrated by considering the behavior of periodic stochastic processes at different scales in an appendix written by the author. This research was completed under the supervision of Prof. Gianni Dal Maso.

We explore the effect of guidance on negativity in the Wigner function representation. Initially, we examine how guidance impact distributions and negative Wigner functions emerge naturally in guided harmonic oscillators. Furthermore, we investigate negativity generation in guided Gaussian states undergoing quadratic evolution. Findings indicate that negative Wigner negativities can arise both in isolated guided Gaussian states and composite systems, including guides with non-zero entropy. This research also demonstrates the connection between guidance and entanglement, revealing that negative Wigner functions and entanglement exhibit a consistent relationship. To assess the practical implications, we investigate the link between guidance, entanglement, and quantum advantage in a guided Bell-like scenario. Results demonstrate that guidance is beneficial for quantum advantage in this context. This research provides a foundation for understanding the role of guidance in quantum properties and negativity within the Wigner function representation. It paves the way for future studies on guidance effects in quantum information applications. The research also highlights the potential of guided quantum systems to exhibit unique properties. Ultimately, this research contributes to the understanding of guidance effects in quantum mechanics. The security of one-time password generation in quantum key distribution is enhanced with a non-uniform random source. However, determining the entropy generated by this source poses a problem, as entropy values are only known to approximate the non-uniform distribution. To address this issue, we develop a method for precisely evaluating the entropy of a non-uniform distribution. Our method involves constructing upper and lower bounds for the entropy by leveraging the source's non-uniformity, and we demonstrate its application in analyzing the security of one-time password generation. Our approach also offers versatility, as it can be applied to diverse source models. Our method allows for precise key generation rate calculation in certain scenarios, and provides a safe and conservative rate estimate in other scenarios. Our study confirms that the key generation rate can be maximized when the non-uniform distribution is known. In addition, we found that the conventional uniform distribution is the most favorable distribution for password generation. Our bound evaluation method is useful for analyzing the security of various password generation schemes, and can be applied in diverse contexts. Furthermore, we developed an algorithm to approximate the optimal non-uniform distribution for password generation, and our experimental results show that the conventional uniform distribution is a suitable default choice when the optimal non-uniform distribution is unknown. Our research provides theoretical support and practical guidance for one-time password generation. And finally, our study reveals that the key generation rate can be enhanced with a non-uniform random source, and our method offers a valuable contribution to password generation analysis. This note employs Faulhaber's Formula to derive alternating odd-degree Bernoulli polynomials, a discovery previously established by Euler using a distinct method. Additionally, it outlines Euler's subsequent demonstration of an identity relating alternating Bernoulli polynomials to the factorial's structure, now understood as a consequence of Faulhaber's work. Finally, both methods are used to prove a related identity for even-degree Bernoulli polynomials. The note concludes by noting the inverse implication: Euler's findings were instrumental in generating Faulhaber's conclusions. The primary objective is to present a sequential explanation of these discoveries, highlighting the inherent beauty and significance of these mathematical findings. As a result, this analysis may serve as a suitable instructional material for presenting these concepts to students. Moreover, this sequence provides a clear illustration of Euler's contribution as a precursor, allowing the examination of how his work was subsequently refined and further developed by other mathematicians. The relevant contributions of Faulhaber, Euler, and even Newton are documented in the appendices for reference. The primary conclusion drawn from this analysis is that Faulhaber's conclusions were fully derived from Euler's earlier findings, but this is not considered an instance of "the piggyback effect" as described by Katerina Iatlova. Rather, the opposite is suggested – Faulhaber offers insight into Euler, which can be characterized as an instance of "inspiration." The paper's final section explores an additional contribution from Newton, which is used to prove Faulhaber's conclusions through an analysis of alternating Bernoulli polynomials at x=1. A major barrier to using reward learning algorithms in the real world is that they require a substantial amount of human time to set up, mainly because they need a significant number of expensive human ratings for every action. To overcome this limitation, we propose a solution by dividing the rating process into two steps. First, we group similar actions based on their visual properties and ask humans to rank the groups. Then, we use the results to create a more efficient action ranking. This approach reduces the number of human ratings needed and makes it possible to use weak labels. Our study shows that our method can handle large action spaces by leveraging the power of visual cues. Using the Atari Games dataset, we demonstrate that our method can achieve better performance with significantly fewer human ratings compared to traditional methods. For instance, we can set up the ratings for over 200 actions in the game "Space Invaders" using only 5 minutes of human time, which is 6 times more efficient than the next best alternative. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study on using visually aided techniques to aid the ratings process for reward learning. As data-driven decision-making proliferates, ensuring that algorithms can be understood by those executing them is becoming increasingly vital.  We propose a comprehensive framework to measure this interpretability, centered on the idea that humans must learn how to execute (or Ground Truth Alterability) and communicate about (or Explanability) algorithms.  We develop a multi-faceted framework combining these aspects and introduce a new metric, the Explanability Ground Truth Alterability Cognitive Intricacy score (EG-ACI), which assesses both the ease of learning an algorithm and explaining its actions.  We present the EG-ACI standard and a variant (EG-ACIv) tailored to scenarios where specific outcomes need to be explained.  We apply the EG-ACI and EG-ACIv to black-box and Deep Learning algorithms, examining their applicability to scenarios where airplanes need to be repaired.  We show that these algorithms are difficult to understand and communicate, indicating a need for improvements in their Ground Truth Alterability and Explanability.  We discuss the implications of our study and suggest future research directions. Hoehn and Dittmann proposed an approach to relativistic hydrodynamics based on Doppler effects in an observer-based frame of reference. Building on their work, we refine their model by addressing a critical flaw, namely the unjustified increase in the number of degrees of freedom, and develop a method to apply it in scenarios where matter distribution meets specific criteria. Leveraging Urimoto's theorem, we establish a condition for the hydrodynamic expansion to be equivalent to the thermodynamic expansion. Furthermore, for cases where matter distribution falls under certain conditions, we derive a novel expansion criterion drawing inspiration from de Sitter's concept. Additionally, in situations where matter distribution falls under certain conditions, we derive a more accurate version of Hoehn and Dittmann's original formula. We also demonstrate that the central objects in our galaxy, such as stars and black holes, do not meet the condition, thereby establishing that the hydrodynamic expansion is not applicable to them. We also apply this condition to electrons in the context of the plasma formed in our galaxy. We observe a similarity between our findings and previous research by other scientists. This paper presents SWIFTER, a pre-processing technique designed to identify concepts
from a large number of execution traces and generate more targeted search terms.
By leveraging crowdsourced labeling to pinpoint key segments in each trace, SWIFTER
uses these segments to create informative sub-traces that serve as a concept dictionary.
A self-learning classifier then applies natural language processing techniques to
determine which sub-traces contain concepts relevant to the overall data set.
Based on these concepts, the query is rephrased to direct more focused index structures
toward sub-traces containing relevant information, while those without concepts are
dismissed or set aside for further analysis. We demonstrate SWIFTER's effectiveness
in concept discovery via experiments with a comprehensive data set from Stack Overflow. 
By integrating the platform's rich metadata, the technique achieves remarkable results,
including a 98% reduction in search time and improved precision of 44% compared to standard
search methods. Our technique is available at https://swifter.fim.uni-lj.si.

Conversational speech analysis is a crucial area of research that has far-reaching applications for both social science and human-centered AI development purposes. Speech synchrony, referring to the timing coherence of speech partners, is a key indicator that reflects the speaker's emotional state, interpersonal relationships, and attention levels. Current methods for estimating synchrony from speech signals often rely on complex and labor-intensive processes. This paper explores the potential of employing deep learning architectures in an unsupervised setting to derive a speech synchrony distance from audio or video recordings. We evaluate the performance of six deep models - including recurrent networks and autoencoders - on two datasets from existing research, one focused on conversational speech between humans and another on human-machine interactions. Our experiments reveal that a model combining recurrent networks and dynamic time warping achieves superior performance compared to other models and traditional speech features in terms of capturing speech synchrony. While our approach demonstrates promising results, it does come with a higher computational overhead compared to previous methods. Nevertheless, the benefits of unsupervised detection and improved accuracy make this approach an attractive option. Future work could focus on scaling up this approach for real-world applications and refining it for analyzing complex speech patterns, such as those found in dialogue marked by frequent interruptions. A key concept in speech research known as speech synchrony has significant implications for our understanding of emotional states, interpersonal dynamics, and attention levels. This study develops a novel method for unsupervised speech synchrony analysis leveraging deep learning and time-series distance measures. We introduce a range of deep models that integrate temporal information, including recurrent networks and multi-layered autoencoders. We evaluate six different deep models and three time-series distance measures on two publicly available speech datasets. Our approach achieves high accuracy in speech synchrony analysis in an unsupervised setting, outperforming previous methods in most cases. We also conduct an in-depth comparison of different deep models and time-series distance measures to provide deeper insights. Our experiment results show that a particular model and measure combination performs best, but the gap in performance between this and other models and measures is relatively small. We also find that reducing the data dimensionality can improve the accuracy of speech synchrony analysis. Our proposed method does, however, come with a higher computational overhead. We conclude that while our approach demonstrates promising results, further research is needed to address computational issues. We suggest exploring more efficient computational architectures and developing methods for analyzing speech in various complex contexts, such as human-machine conversations. Domain adaptation is a critical issue in developing adaptable models across different regions. The source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) challenge, which involves adapting a model without access to the source domain, is particularly significant in this area. Typically, SFDA relies on prior knowledge or a small amount of labeled data from the target domain to compensate for the lack of source domain data. However, when access to target domain labeled data is also restricted, SFDA becomes even more challenging. To address this problem, we propose a new SFDA approach that involves transferring ideas from unsupervised domains. This approach utilizes theories to capture the underlying meanings of class names and creates pseudo-labels for developing theory-consistent features. Additionally, we propose a method for combining different theories to reduce class imbalance problems. By combining theory-based pseudo-labels and class balance techniques with a single supervised head, we are able to achieve state-of-the-art results on several domain adaptation datasets, which has allowed us to improve the state-of-the-art on SFDA datasets by over 4% and expand the applicability of SFDA to multiple unsupervised domains. The code for this project is available on the link: https://github.com/Confident2023/SFNet. Additionally, our experiments demonstrate that pseudo-labels can effectively facilitate domain adaptation across multiple unsupervised domains and highlight the significance of selecting relevant theories for improving SFDA performance. A Gas Core Reactor could revolutionize nuclear power for deep space missions, potentially surpassing traditional Gas Top Reactors in several areas. With its reactor core made entirely of fuel, the GCR offers a large amount of energy relative to its mass and can operate at various thermal energy levels, ranging from 0.5 to 2.0 keV. This thermal flexibility allows the reactor to be paired with various heat exchangers and Brayton cycles, enabling optimization for specific mission requirements. Notably, a 250 kW GCR has been demonstrated to achieve impressive performance milestones, including a thermal efficiency of 34% and over 370,000 specific impulse. This report examines various GCR energy conversion systems and assesses their capabilities for different space missions. A system-level analysis of the GCR energy conversion system is carried out using the NASA LEAP tool, which evaluates performance, risks, and schedule factors. Several system design options are presented, each featuring its own unique set of trade-offs.
