A universal Bellman equation is applied to solve the n-step value function for any Markov decision process, using only the current moment and a finite history. This provides the basis to develop a real-time n-step evaluation method for MDPs with finite states and actions. Next, we establish conditions under which an exponential convergence rate of the error occurs when approximating the n-step value function using an iterative method. This is achieved by combining the Bellman equation with a contraction-like property. Using matrix calculations, we numerically verify this result. Building on these insights, we adapt these concepts to develop an online learning algorithm for MDPs with finite states and actions, using function approximations based on neural networks. This involves modifying the Bellman backpropagation method to incorporate a history buffer and a regularization term, to capture long-term correlations in MDPs. Moreover, we demonstrate the potential of these methods in hedging and portfolio optimization tasks with time-series models that exhibit long-term memory. This is done by comparing them to state-of-the-art approaches, including reinforcement learning and quantile regression neural networks, as well as a hedging strategy grounded in reinforcement learning but lacking the capacity to analyze long-term patterns. As a result, we observe significant improvements in the performance of the methods with the Bellman properties. This is especially evident in the cases with long-term memory, where the reinforcement learning strategy yields up to 79% lower value of the n-step risk for models with significant persistence. The source code for these experiments can be found at https://github.com/andreaspillmann/profound-bellman-hedging. The results suggest that incorporating the Bellman properties and an online learning process with a history buffer and a regularization term can be very beneficial in MDPs, especially those with long-term memory. This is despite the potential drawbacks of delayed gratification, higher computational requirements, and larger function classes. The methods are further validated by their success in the portfolio optimization task, where the performance is in line with the risk-neutral results. Recommender systems still face a major issue in accurately predicting user motivation. Most current approaches fail to generalize this important variable due to its inherent variability and scarcity in data. In an effort to overcome this challenge, we introduce an innovative framework called Hidden User Motivation Modeling for Recommender Systems. This model differentiates itself by modeling the underlying user motivation as a sequence of states rather than a static state. Additionally, it leverages a novel attention-based mechanism over multiple interaction history channels to effectively capture the varying motivations of users. Motivation labels are not always available in real-time, so we also present a novel technique for imputing these labels. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in accurately predicting user motivation. Motivation labels can be used to improve a variety of downstream recommendations. This work was made possible by a benchmark dataset containing explicit motivation labels, called Moto, which was developed for e-commerce product recommendations. Our model won first place in the MMS 2021 Challenge on Motivation Modeling in Recommender Systems. Our code can be found at https://github.com/zy19937107796/HUM. This research has been published in a paper titled "Hidden Motion Modeling for Recommenders" and has appeared at the 2021 ACM Conference on Information and Knowledge Management. A related paper titled "Motion-Aware Recommendation" has also been presented at the 2022 IEEE International Conference on Data Engineering and Intelligent Computing. In statistical analysis, matrix approximation finds a wide range of practical uses in enhancing estimation precision for variables affected by heteroscedasticity. This comes in two forms: (1) when the variance of observations is known and uneven, requiring matrix division, and (2) when variances are unknown and group-wise heterogeneous, requiring weightings for accurate estimates. Research has thoroughly explored the consequences of uneven variance on the estimates in (1), but similar exploration for group-wise heterogeneity in (2) is relatively less done. We explore three scenarios involving matrix approximation with group-wise heterogeneity in regressions and identify the critical conditions under which they work. Our study utilizes simulations and an empirical analysis to verify our theoretical predictions, showing that these conditions define the essential boundaries within which matrix heterogeneity functions seamlessly. This research further demonstrates that, beyond these limits, matrix heterogeneity exhibits more complex behaviors. We also demonstrate that, under specific conditions, the performance of matrix heterogeneity is contingent upon the level of group-wise heterogeneity, a factor not previously considered in regression analysis with uneven variances. This study contributes to the development of more accurate and refined statistical analysis methods by pinpointing the critical conditions for successful matrix heterogeneity in group-wise regression analysis. We demonstrate that these conditions can be estimated through direct, model-free methods which are easy to implement and improve with increasing sample sizes. Such estimators show consistent and strong relationships with the outcomes, an aspect not observed in our simulations and empirical analysis. This study further explores the potential of using these estimators in detecting uneven group-wise heterogeneity. We demonstrate that these conditions can be achieved not only through the use of matrix heterogeneity but also through the application of group-wise weighted analysis with correctly chosen weights. Our simulations and empirical observations, however, reveal that, beyond these limits, group-wise weighted analysis exhibits more complex behaviors. We observe, for example, that, beyond these limits, group-wise weighted analysis may fail to achieve even group-wise heterogeneity, a failure not seen in our simulations and empirical analysis. This paper explores the development of distributed control strategies for networked systems, focusing on regulating individual channel states or combining them into optimized outcomes. For each objective, we devise and analyze two control algorithms: a centralized, adaptive approach that adjusts channel inputs to regulate the target variable, and a decentralized method that instead adjusts interconnection weights between channels to achieve regulation. In both cases, we examine stability and convergence times, demonstrating that the convergence rates of the decentralized strategy match those of its centralized counterpart. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the system's behavior, from initial convergence to long-term performance, and show that local control allows for greater system resilience, faster convergence, and robustness to disturbances. Our study also reveals that the convergence rates of the decentralized strategy are solely dependent on system properties, eliminating the need for online computations. Instead, these can be performed offline, reducing online computational load. We extend this study by exploring optimization methods, showing that the decentralized strategy can efficiently achieve a variety of goals with minimal adjustments to interconnection weights, thus enhancing its overall performance and robustness. Overall, our research provides a foundation for understanding and improving distributed control systems, from fundamental principles to complex applications. These principles can be applied to a broad range of systems, from multi-channel to more complex models, and demonstrate the potential for scalable and adaptable control architectures. Many robotic tasks are hindered by inadequate perception due to insufficient or
outdated labels in traditional supervised learning methods. These methods necessitate
exhaustive data collection, involving both environmental interaction and manual
annotation. To overcome this limitation, we propose leveraging human expertise in
a different manner – by delegating tasks to crowd-sourced evaluators and employing
automated aggregation techniques to produce high-quality labels. Our proposed Voting
-based Automatic Urban Environment enrichment algorithm (VALUE) efficiently
generates comprehensive annotations for significant urban features, such as buildings,
roads, and vegetation, over large scales. Our evaluation shows that the resultant
annotations produced minimal errors in three significant scenarios – localization,
feature extraction, and scene understanding – comparable to those obtained through
expensive manual labeling. These high-quality labels are further utilized to facilitate
the understanding and interpretation of unstructured outdoor environments. As an
example of its applicability, VALUE is applied to supporting drone-based construction
inspection services. To promote the reproducibility of our work, we publicly share

In seismic imaging, deconvolving reflection waves is crucial and traditionally done using conventional methods like matrix inversion or l1 regularization. However, these methods have drawbacks, as matrix inversion can be computationally expensive and l1 regularization may not utilize the inherent patterns within the waves. To address these issues, we propose a new nonuniform sparse deconvolution approach called NuSPAN, which learns a proximal mean network that combines l1 regularization with learned regression for inherent pattern extraction. By differentiating between l1 regularization and learned regression, NuSPAN achieves better reconstruction results. Experimental results demonstrate NuSPAN's superiority over existing techniques in reconstructing seismic reflections. Notably, it outperforms a state-of-the-art l1 regularization method and shows greater robustness to noise in both synthetic and real-world reflection data. Additionally, NuSPAN's applicability extends beyond deconvolution tasks, making it a versatile tool for other sparse-related problems. In particular, we determine the dominant universal contribution to the excitations in the Haagerup model and find that the leading universal term matches the previously observed Bethe-Yang level-4 excitations. For decades, researchers have been working on annotating historical texts with part-of-speech tags. Despite significant advancements in automatic POS labeling, systematic errors persist, particularly in datasets that are scarce or have complex syntax. As a result, some classes tend to be overrepresented at the expense of others, leading to unreliable labeling. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel method for revising automatic POS labels, based on the idea of set-valued outputs. This approach takes into account that multiple POS labels can be associated with a single word, depending on its context. By leveraging existing automatic labeling and revising pairs from annotated subsets, we can effectively correct systematic errors and achieve more accurate labeling, all within a principled Bayesian framework. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms alternative correction techniques in terms of accuracy and robustness. Furthermore, when applied to the Early New English Corpus and the Typerighter Corpus, it results in significant improvements, correcting 27.6% and 41.3% of automatic labels, respectively. To facilitate future research, we release our implementation on GitHub, along with corrected labels for ENHC and TCL. Moreover, we outline a feasible pathway for making our system applicable to other datasets. Ultimately, our research shows that there is potential for correcting errors in existing POS labels, potentially even revising labels for the Penn-Hist corpus to make them dependable once more. In a regular category, a preorder can be visualized as a subobject that has no conflicts or clashes, equivalently as a subobject that is completely cohesive and inclusive. A equivalence relation in such a category can be depicted as a subobject that is not only uniquely cohesive and invariant. We introduce a cocartesian depiction of preorders and equivalence relations in a regular category and examine the equivalence relation properties that correspond to specific subobject properties. We particularly concentrate on the relationships between reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity in equivalence relations in this context. We establish that certain subobject properties corresponding to these relations exist in any regular category. We introduce a specific type of subobject called binary, applicable to pairs, and demonstrate its use in illustrating equivalence relations properties. We also discuss how this binary depiction simplifies equivalence relation properties in categories with pullbacks. We ultimately explore applications of this approach in the context of topoi. We illustrate the use of this method in the specific examples of the categories of topological spaces, uniform spaces, and uniform spaces with the Hausdorff property. We demonstrate that the subobject depiction of preorders and equivalence relations in a regular category encompasses and generalizes several key results in the theory of topological equivalence relations, including the subobject representation of complete linear orders in topological spaces, the existence of symmetry and transitivity relations in regular categories, the correspondence between regular equivalence relations and total relations in topoi, and the generalization of the correspondence between complete orders and equivalence relations in topoi. (The corresponding mathematical theory of topoi developed after the initial writing of this text.) We introduce a specific type of total relation, applicable to total orders, that is particular to topoi. We demonstrate applications of this theory to the context of topoi by proving that certain properties of total relations corresponding to equivalence relations in topoi exist in total orders. We also prove that the subobject depiction of preorders and equivalence relations in a regular category generalizes several key results in the theory of topoi concerning total relations. Among these, an acute-angle lensing event is characterized by its ring-like perturbations, often caused by a foreground star's close binary nature or, more commonly, by a planet. Given the high frequency of planets in such configurations when considering all planets detectable by observation, an expected shortage of such planets in actual cases must imply the prevalence of unaccounted detection mechanisms. These mechanisms, known as secondary effects, can detect remaining planet signals not identified through primary methods, thus playing a crucial role in the comprehensive understanding of planets studied through microlensing. Leveraging the analysis of data from KMT-2018-AE-001 and KMT-2018-AE-008, and employing Planet, a leading planet detection software, our research involved analyzing these two events using five distinct models: four theoretical models incorporating secondary effects and varying levels of consideration for these mechanisms, and one model solely considering primary factors. Our research resulted in the identification of four planets, two of which were known and two newly discovered: the newly discovered planets had masses equivalent to Cb and Cd types. These findings, coupled with an analysis comparing the effectiveness of models incorporating secondary effects to those that do not, reveal the significant influence of such mechanisms in studying planets through microlensing. Moreover, our research marks the completion of a substantial sample of 57 microlensing planets discovered through KMTNet, a leading project, and our analysis suggests the potential for further discoveries with ongoing projects. Ultimately, these discoveries hold great promise for future exoplanet discoveries through this groundbreaking method. The primary function of convolutions in convolutional neural networks is to capture features
based on local spatial context, while also considering orientation. Traditionally, this
orientation consideration is achieved implicitly through the use of specific convolution
kernels that account for the contextual relationships in input data. Nonetheless, it becomes
clear that explicit orientation consideration is essential for capturing features and this
explicitness is crucial for improving convolutions. This is where Orientation Convolutive
Networks come in, allowing for the orientation to be taken into consideration when defining
the convolution operation. This approach leverages the symmetry of convolutions to facilitate
explicit orientation consideration. By doing this, OCNet is capable of enhancing the
network's capabilities, thereby improving its overall performance in image classification. 
Experimental results demonstrate OCNet to be superior to existing top-notch networks in
image classification tasks, particularly when evaluated across datasets including CIFAR100,
Tiny ImageNet, ImageNet and STL10. Additionally, OCNet is noted for its efficiency and
parameter efficiency. Code for OCNet can be found on our GitHub repository at 
https://github.com/chenyimingoo/OCNet. Our code has been awarded a first place prize at
the 2021 IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems journal's competition. 
A related paper titled 'Orientation Convolutive Networks for Image Classification' has been
published at IJCAI'20, where a detailed explanation of OCNet can be found.

To create a long-term, panoramic view from a single perspective has been a difficult challenge in machine learning. Prior approaches were often limited by their inability to maintain a direct view or their small training datasets, resulting in significant distortion in generated images. In this study, we introduce a novel method called DiffDreamer, based on a conditional diffusion system, that generates high-quality, single-view panoramic images from perspective shots. By incorporating a 360-degree latent representation module that ensures a seamless and undistorted view generation, we greatly improved the direct view generation quality and surpassed previous results. Our method achieves an impressive gain of 10.43 and 6.59 in SSIM and PSNR over the best prior approaches, while also outperforming them significantly in visual quality. Additionally, our method allows the generated images to closely resemble the original images in training, and we observe a similar distribution between the original and generated images in testing, indicating its robustness. Our method's source code and datasets are available for public access.  The generated images are showcased in the Panorama Generation Gallery.  Our method's performance is demonstrated in the Perpetual View Generation Gallery.  The source code can also be directly accessed through the GitHub link. This study introduces a novel data-driven framework centered on systems without a priori models, capable of handling linear time-invariant (LTI) and nonlinear dynamic systems alike. The proposed method integrates a universal approximator with an extended Kalman filter to estimate both system states and unknown parameters in multiple output dynamic systems. To address the challenges posed by nonlinearities, the design incorporates a sliding mode approach, allowing the estimator to be resilient to approximation errors while maintaining stability. Differing from existing research, the new framework leverages black-box learning for prediction, and uses optimization-based techniques grounded in observed data, thus circumventing the need for model-based analysis. The proposed methods are demonstrated by numerical simulations using the networked susceptible-infected-susceptible epidemic model. These simulations showcase the framework's capabilities for state estimation, parameter recovery, epidemic outbreak prevention, and control design. Results indicate that the framework can effectively prevent epidemic outbreaks given limited control actions. Additionally, the framework's performance is compared to that of the unscented Kalman filter, and its parameters are adaptively adjusted using single-hidden-layer neural networks to optimize performance. The study concludes by examining the impact of network topology on epidemic control, revealing that the location of infected nodes significantly affects epidemic control. The proposed methods hold promise for a range of applications, including autonomous driving, robotics, and epidemic control, among others. The corresponding code is publicly available at https://github.com/feng1l3/Neural-network-based-data-driven-design-for-networked-systems. The Hunter-Saxton equation primarily concerns the movement of one-dimensional sheets of cells such as epithelial or mesenchymal cells. Solutions to this equation exhibit Lipschitz continuity, specifically $\alpha$-Lipschitz continuity for some $\alpha \geq 0$. We've established that this continuity, or lack thereof, influences the long-term behavior of solutions. In cases where $\alpha > 0$, we've found that solutions remain stable for an infinite amount of time. On the other hand, when $\alpha = 0$, we've discovered that solutions eventually become smooth and develop a finite speed of propagation over time. We've also found that the development of this speed is determined by a particular equation involving the solution's initial Lipschitz continuity. Our analysis relies on the relationship between H\"older continuous H\"older norms and the Hunter-Saxton equation's Hamiltonian structure. We've successfully proven the development of this speed through energy estimates and stability arguments. We've also found an intuitive explanation for the emergence of this speed through geometric and physical considerations related to the transport of active molecules. Furthermore, our analysis also explores the behavior of solutions that have a finite amount of Lipschitz continuity. We demonstrate the existence of solutions with a specific amount of Lipschitz continuity, or $\alpha$-Lipschitz continuity for some $\alpha \geq 0$, using a variational method. We show that these solutions remain stable for an infinite amount of time, or in cases where $\alpha = 0$, they eventually develop a finite speed of propagation. These findings are confirmed through numerical simulations. We also extend our analysis to a more general class of equations that are related to the Hunter-Saxton equation. We demonstrate the emergence of these generalized equations through a reduction principle in dynamical systems. Our analysis also explores the implications of our results for the dynamics of 2D active layers. We show that the behavior of 2D active layers can be reduced to a 1D model, or a set of effective 1D equations. Our analysis also reveals how the speed of 1D active layers is influenced by factors such as the solution's initial conditions and its complex microstructure. Evaluating scoliosis with ultrasound imaging can be a challenging task, especially when done manually, as it requires significant experience and manual dexterity to obtain accurate measurements of spinal curvature. A more reliable approach has been explored through robotic scanning technology, which can automatically gather reliability and accuracy in scoliosis evaluation. To compare the effectiveness of manual and robotic scanning, patients with scoliosis who had previously undergone posterior correction surgery underwent both manual and robotic scanning procedures. The results showed that robotic scanning yielded high interobserver and intraobserver reliability, comparable to manual scanning, and Robotic scanning produced correlation coefficients of 0.94-0.96 for major curves, outperforming manual scanning with coefficients of 0.64-0.76. Additionally, robotic scanning demonstrated greater accuracy in measuring coronal view Cobb angles for major curves (mean difference ranging from -0.3 to 0.3 degrees) in comparison to coronal view manual scanning (mean difference ranging from -3.3 to 7.3 degrees). By automating spinal curvature measurement with enhanced precision and reliability, robotic scanning has the potential to improve scoliosis evaluation and treatment. Overall, robotic scanning emerged as a superior method for scoliosis diagnosis and treatment planning. Video supplementary material is available online. Recent advancements in MIMO architecture have led to impressive performance in natural language processing tasks. However, the separate attention mechanisms in each encoder and decoder module hinder end-to-end optimization during training. To overcome this limitation, we introduce Effective Feature Sharing (EFS), a novel method that enables the sharing of feature views, though not attention weights, between cross-attention blocks in MIMO structures. By EFS, each encoder and decoder module can now process the same feature views, including historical and future information, while reducing feature redundancy. The proposed EFS is compatible with existing MIMO models and can be easily integrated without training adjustments. Experimental results demonstrate that EFS improves the accuracy of MIMO models by 0.3-1.2% on benchmark datasets, including GLUE and CoNLL-2003. Notably, EFS surpasses the current state-of-the-art performance in several cases. The source code is available at https://github.com/klkutukop/effective-feature-sharing.

This work introduces weighted contexts, a class of directed metric spaces equipped with an authority function that surpasses just existence. For every weighted context that meets certain criteria, we establish the existence of a unique optimal framework, comprising directed paths and cycles with calculated weights, that mirrors the original space's geometry. This optimal framework is then characterized as a weighted metric interval category, capturing the weighted context's essential directional and metric properties. To prove this result, we first demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of a metric interval category in every weighted context that meets specific criteria, and then show that the optimal framework's properties align with the weighted context's directions and metrics. As a consequence of our method, we prove the existence and uniqueness of a metric interval category in every weighted space, and thus generalize a recent result obtained through a different approach. Our method also yields new insights into the properties of optimal frameworks and the weighted metric interval categories within weighted contexts, including the need for authority functions in optimal framework definitions. While there are various noise-reduction mechanisms, many of them assume that the source and degree of noise are known in advance. However, in real-world situations, this is not typically the case. In this study, we examined the use of the Bayesian Statistics Directed mechanism in conjunction with the Label Renovation Mechanism to investigate the effect of label noise and develop a method to counteract it. Furthermore, we applied these methods to a challenging task, namely, medical image categorization, which involves predicting four critical medical conditions (CMCs). We utilized the 30,000 images from the Comparative Study of Deep Learning Diagrams (CSDLD) dataset to demonstrate the practical application of these methods. In doing so, we discovered that the Label Renovation Mechanism is effective up to a point, but its performance degrades as the level of noise increases. In contrast, the Bayesian Statistics Directed mechanism outperforms other baseline models even in scenarios with high levels of noise. Lastly, through our analysis, we identified the L1 regularization method as the most effective label noise-reduction strategy among the ones examined. In summary, our research highlights the importance of considering label noise and suggests the use of L1 regularization to mitigate its impact in medical image categorization tasks. The presence of interparticle forces other than van der Waals or electrostatic may account for the excessive stiffness observed in granular matter. However, the nature of these forces remains unclear. To address this, we've studied a system consisting of submillimeter silica particles in a 0-100 mT magnetic field where the magnetization-induced dipole interactions clearly cause the stiffness to increase with concentration. To counterbalance the dipole moments, a opposing force is applied due to magnetic field-induced anisotropic stress, supporting the anomalous screening theory proposed by Kresch and Chayes. This theory suggests that concentration-dependent mechanical properties are influenced by a collective mechanism. To further investigate this, we measured the stress transfer between adjacent particles and found that the mechanical bonds switch between static and dynamic states in a concentration-dependent manner, with lower concentrations exhibiting static bonds and higher concentrations exhibiting lower static bond ratios and increased dynamic bonds. This study supports the anomalous screening theory, proposing that a concentration-dependent critical concentration exist where mechanical stability is affected by a collective mechanism changeover. To achieve such a screening transition shift, a specific design of granular materials is proposed. These materials can remain stable at low concentrations due to magnetization-induced dipole interactions, transition into an unstable region at intermediate concentrations due to increased dynamic bonds, and become stable again at higher concentrations due to opposing interparticle forces. Our research supports the idea of a universal screening transition in granular materials and provides a framework for understanding the role of various interparticle forces. To further investigate this, we've studied the mechanical properties of colloidal suspensions consisting of 2 micrometer silica particles in a shear flow, where the shear stress is found to increase linearly with concentration up to a critical concentration, exceeding which the shear stress suddenly drops. This critical concentration is found to be identical to the critical concentration of the Manning model, describing a screening transition shift in materials with a highly concentrated mechanical behavior. To explain these findings, we've demonstrated that the highly concentrated interparticle forces are capable of inducing a mechanical behavior changeover, existing in parallel with existing interparticle forces. This changeover is found to be the key to understanding the highly concentrated mechanical behavior of granular matter and supports the idea of a universal screening transition shift in materials with a highly concentrated mechanical behavior. Together, our studies support the idea of a universal screening transition shift in materials with a highly concentrated mechanical behavior, existing in both granular matter and suspension matter, and influenced by different types of interparticle forces. Artificial oversampling, which involves generating synthetic instances for underprivileged classes, has emerged as an effective means to improve data balance and performance. In this study, we explored the application of artificial oversampling techniques, including one-nearest neighbor, decision tree, k-nearest neighbor, and Bayesian learning, to enhance classification accuracy in imbalanced data sets. Our findings suggest that the proposed oversampling technique has the potential to enhance text categorization performance without significant computational costs. Notably, some TV news channels focused more on the health and economic impacts than others, particularly when reporting on hotspots with high infection rates and deaths. This study examines the connections between regional news coverage, COVID-19 cases and deaths, and audience numbers, using a dataset that combines a content analysis, epidemiological data, and audience metrics from 4,664 TV news segments from 47 U.S. states. The rapid multipole method is a variant of the algorithm traditionally used to speed up computations of N-body simulations by decoupling close pairs of bodies and handling their interactions separately. This accelerated approach relies on approximating higher-order interactions to achieve increased performance benefits. However, it inherently introduces uncertainties, specifically errors in conserving physical quantities like angular momentum due to its approximation methods. Our investigation focuses on quantifying these inaccuracies in angular momentum preservation for pairs of bodies with free and constrained movement. Our results show that angular momentum errors in the free case follow an inverse proportionality relationship with the approximation factor used, while for constrained motion, errors remain constant with regards to that factor. These findings serve to clarify the impact of approximations in one specific algorithm on a fundamental physical property and can be extended to explore potential discrepancies in other quantities. Our code for these calculations can be found at https://github.com/krzysztofzabka/AHMC_test. Additionally, we've adapted the accurate algorithm, resulting in negligible performance losses but ensured conservation of angular momentum, making it suitable for precise simulations, like planetary ephemeris calculations or moon phase predictions. Our study also suggests that the approximated algorithm can still produce acceptable results for applications focused on moon phase prediction alone. However, the exact algorithm should be used for high-precision applications related to fundamental celestial body dynamics. Our study offers the following key implications: the approximated algorithm should not be used for constraints where angular momentum preservation is critical, and for the self-gravitating case, the approximated algorithm can produce acceptable results in moon phase prediction scenarios only. Our study also offers a critical benchmark for performance loss vs conservation of angular momentum, showing that in our specific case, a 30% slowdown in accuracy was required to achieve a 0.1% improvement in angular momentum conservation. Current machine learning methods primarily rely on observational data to derive insights. However, using only observational data can limit a model's capabilities, as compared to having direct access to a knowledgeable authority. In this paper, we explore a concept where we augment the available data using transformations that preserve its inherent properties. By doing so, we demonstrate that even a machine learning model without prior knowledge can still effectively learn from a knowledgeable authority when given sufficient data. Our research showcases that these ideals can be achieved in the context of statistical learning. Specifically, we present a set of data amplification functions based on vector projections and show that they can enhance any authority's performance, resulting in optimal outcomes under specific conditions. Additionally, we explore the theoretical underpinnings of data amplification and discuss its practical applications, including its potential to improve performance even with limited knowledge. Ultimately, our research paves the way for developing new methods to augment data drawn from knowledgeable authorities. The results of this project were also presented at the International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Data Science (AI-4S 2021). It particularly examines how pattern characteristics can be understood through changes in pattern size as the period changes, and highlights length-related phenomena in non-periodic patterns that are influenced by their periodic structures. Individuals holding lower-income positions tended to engage in a more restricted range of activities, have fewer choices of routes, and visit fewer destinations. Their reduced mobility was largely due to limited access to private vehicles. Following the pandemic, lower-income urban travelers found themselves in an even more disadvantaged position relative to their higher-income counterparts, highlighting the urgent need to re-evaluate the structure of urban transportation and interaction post-pandemic. The study of multiphase flows in complex media gains importance due to its broad applicability across oil reservoir modeling and geothermal energy extraction. Achieving efficient and stable numerical resolutions of these complex systems poses significant challenges. A new approach, known as TWINS, has been developed to alleviate these difficulties by applying global pressure and split flow variables. This method employs a fully implicit time-stepping scheme and a Newton-type iteration to solve the coupled system of equations. However, the efficiency and stability of TWINS depend heavily on initial guesses for pressure and Navier-Stokes equations resolution. Drawing inspiration from multiphase flow formulations, TWINS has been adapted to include multiple pressure types and initial guesses based on expert knowledge. This research compares the performance of TWINS with and without prior pressure guesses derived from streamline methods and by using an unsplit pressure scheme as an alternative solution. TWINS has been successfully applied to test cases representing a range of increasing complexity from single-phase flow in homogeneous media to two-phase flow in heterogeneous media with and without the presence of wells. TWINS' performance has been evaluated based on convergence speed, stability, and accuracy of results. A thorough analysis of method performance and areas for improvement has also been conducted. This research provides valuable insights and guidance for numerical analysts and engineers working with multiphase flow simulations. Furthermore, TWINS has significant potential as a versatile simulator capable of addressing a variety of problems in reservoir modeling and beyond. This study offers a foundation for further method development and general-purpose simulation applications. This research primarily focuses on method development and demonstration, and a companion paper will explore the application and utilization of TWINS in practical settings and detailed case studies. TWINS is planned to be released as an open-source software package in the future. Several key test cases are currently available on GitHub within the TWINS repository. TWINS' source code is also available on GitHub within the reservoir-simulations repository. TWINS has been successfully tested on a range of Linux and Unix-based operating systems including Ubuntu and macOS. TWINS has been successfully compiled with CMake and has been successfully executed on a range of processors including x86, aarch64, and powerpc. The interfacial surface is modeled as a single plane of uniform charge rather than a more complex arrangement of layers. The standard approach assumes a non-deformable interface and neglects the impact of electrostatic potential on dipole moments associated with ions and the interfacial material. In contrast, our approach takes into account the dynamic response of the electrolyte solvent to changes in electrostatic potential and the resulting dipole moments. These considerations have significant effects on EDL behavior when the interfacial surface charge density is relatively low. A key feature of our approach is the use of generalized Kirkwood-Roig-Frigola potential to describe solvent polarization. The results show that solvent polarization plays a crucial role in determining EDL properties such as capacitance, zeta potential, and ion distribution near the interfacial plane. Advancements in LiDAR technology have significantly enhanced autonomous vehicle perception capabilities, particularly for obstacle detection and navigation purposes. Self-supervised learning has emerged as a valuable strategy for fine-tuning perception models, given the difficulty and expense of acquiring labeled data. However, existing self-supervised methods for autonomous vehicle perception often rely on sequence-based approaches, leading to potential prejudices that can hinder performance, such as scene and velocity dependencies. This study introduces an innovative self-supervised method for improving deep neural network (DNN) filters in multi-sensor fusion, particularly for vehicle pose estimation. We focus on an autonomous driving task - cross-distribution scan matching - and explore ways to detect and minimize prejudices, identifying self-supervised strategies and potential performance enhancements. Furthermore, we propose a DNN filter approach to prevent prejudice effects and analyze its performance across various distribution sizes. Our experimental results, based on 13 distinct datasets, demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method and suggest several potential research avenues. This study is expected to contribute significantly to the development of robust and prejudice-resistant self-supervised methods for autonomous vehicle perception. Such advancements will be crucial for enhancing perception system reliability and reducing development costs. Ultimately, the goal is to create more efficient and effective self-supervised methods that can overcome prejudice limitations and significantly improve performance. To validate this vision, we plan to conduct extensive testing and analysis to identify and address specific prejudice effects and customize our approach to accommodate unique prejudice patterns. For instance, sequence-based prejudice can be mitigated by incorporating a global feature extractor to improve model robustness, while cross-distribution prejudice can be alleviated by introducing a local feature extractor to determine relevant distributions. By taking these measures, we are confident that our approach can lead to substantial performance enhancements and contribute valuable insights to the self-supervised learning community. This study is expected to open up new possibilities for self-supervised learning in the context of autonomous vehicle perception and may inspire the development of similar techniques for other applications where prejudice can hinder performance. One such application could be self-supervised learning for medical image analysis, where prejudice could arise due to differences in data collection protocols and impact model generalizability. In such cases, prejudice mitigation methods like those presented in this study could significantly improve performance and contribute valuable insights to the self-supervised learning and prejudice mitigation communities. This study is expected to lay the groundwork for future research in prejudice mitigation and self-supervised learning for medical image analysis. By applying our approach to this application domain, we may be able to improve the effectiveness of self-supervised learning for medical image analysis

Edge detection is a fundamental task in satellite imagery processing, and for
expert analysts working with images, being able to perform this task quickly and
efficiently is crucial. To support these professionals in their daily work, we
evaluate and compare the performance of three popular edge detection algorithms,
namely Canny, Sobel, and Logarithmic Sobel, against a state-of-the-art deep
network model. Our analysis shows that the Canny method delivers the best overall
results, while the Sobel approach offers a faster processing speed. Interestingly,
the combination of the logarithmic transformation with the Sobel operator has
merits of its own, and surprisingly, when applied on real satellite images, can
surpass the performance of the Canny method. Ultimately, we suggest that the Canny
method be used for ideal conditions, while the logarithmic Sobel approach be
utilized for coping with noisy images. To provide a comprehensive comparison,
we have created a dedicated webpage with detailed results and graphical
visualizations. Our methodology is further documented in a GitHub repository,
where our code and data are freely accessible. In addition, we provide an

Automated segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions from brain scans has been developed over the years, with newer models outperforming older ones. A key challenge is that these models are often optimized for specific datasets and may not function well in other collections. One potential solution is to train neural networks continuously, updating them with new data from different sources to improve their performance. However, this approach also requires careful consideration of the impact of new data on the model's existing performance. Our study compares the effectiveness of training models from scratch versus updating them with new data on the task of lesion segmentation. We used data from three MS lesion segmentation challenges - MSSEG 2016, BRATS2015, and a private dataset from St. Michael's Hospital - to train models, and then tested them on each other to evaluate their performance. Our results show that training models continuously can be an efficient way to improve their performance on new tasks, with one model trained on two datasets showing better performance than models trained from scratch on individual datasets. Overall, our study finds that training models continuously is a promising approach for updating existing models and improving their performance on a wide range of clinical datasets. Recent advances in machine learning and modeling have led to accelerated
resolution of longstanding problems in physics and geophysics, thanks to
combined efforts of human expertise and AI capabilities. Nonetheless, models
developed through machine learning sometimes yield results contradicting or
ignoring established knowledge. Determining when to trust learned model outputs
requires a deeper understanding of potential mistakes in machine-learned
models. In the context of dynamical systems, pinpointing regime boundaries
constitutes a challenging task for both machines and humans. This study aims to
establish a framework for identifying mistakes in machine-learned models by
combining quantitative measures of model accuracy, trust regions, and critical
boundaries. We will detail the development of a reliable model assessment
procedure, test its efficacy on a numerical control problem, and discuss how
this framework can be applied to other complex systems. This research will provide
the foundation for guiding machines and humans in conjunction for joint problem
solving in modeling and physics. We will also discuss ways to rectify mistakes
detected during model assessment. We envision this framework to be versatile and
applicable to other fields and domains requiring collaborative machine-learning
assistance. We will present the framework as a structured lesson, complete with
code demonstrations, educational examples, and sample applications. This work
will contribute to enhancing the quality of machine learning and modeling
produced in conjunction between machines and humans. We will also provide code
samples for educational and research purposes. We plan to further develop and
refine this framework in conjunction with researchers from materials science,
physics, and geophysics who may identify novel applications and contributions.

The formation of massive stars is thought to occur in dense cores that have undergone catastrophic collapse. Researchers have discovered what they believe is a dense core in the process of collapsing to form a massive star. The core, which is about 0.01 times the mass of our sun, is located in the Carina Nebula and is being studied using data collected from different wavelengths. The data show that the core is moving at a consistent speed and is experiencing shock waves as it interacts with its surroundings. The researchers believe this core may have formed through the evaporation of dust grains that are rich in heavy elements. The area around the core is also home to numerous smaller cores that are still in the early stages of formation. These smaller cores are too small to collapse and may be an indicator of an even larger, gas-rich cloud that contains the massive core. We're investigating how representatives of businesses find and hire professionals suitable for tasks such as creating summaries online, a process that can be challenging due to a large pool of available workers. We analyzed the difficulties encountered by two companies, CrowdSource and Cognigy, in hiring summarizers on Amazon's Mechanical Turk platform. We evaluated the effectiveness of using various qualifications - both technical and behavioral - in identifying qualified summarizers by analyzing over 1,000 requests for specific tasks. Our results show that while certain technical qualifications can improve the relevance of worker selections, they do not guarantee high task completion rates. Moreover, companies may need to adapt their hiring processes in response to changes in the availability of skilled workers. Therefore, we recommend that companies of similar size adapt and adjust their own hiring procedures rather than solely relying on pre-established criteria. Additionally, we suggest exploring new methods of talent discovery and acquisition within the talent market to mitigate the issues associated with identifying qualified summarizers. Text-video retrieval has gained significant attention due to its potential real-world applications, such as video captioning and browsing. Current methods use advanced models like BERT and Longformer to establish a common understanding between text and video. However, computing complex attention matrices and token representations are resource-intensive and limit the model's capacity to process long sequences. To overcome these limitations, we introduce TS2-Net, a novel transformer model that addresses these challenges through token shifting and choice. Token shifting allows the model to focus on temporal and contextual information by averaging adjacent frames' tokens, reducing the need for high-resolution video inputs. Additionally, we implement a choice mechanism that prunes attention matrices and reduce memory requirements, enabling the model to efficiently process long sequences. We achieve this through a novel approach called Local-Global Sampled Attention (LGSA). We evaluate TS2-Net on various datasets, including activity recognition, video question answering, and text-video retrieval, demonstrating its state-of-the-art performance and efficiency. Experiments show that TS2-Net's efficiency stems from its ability to leverage contextual information from adjacent frames. We release the model's source code on GitHub. Analyses based on different pruning techniques, attention matrix pruning rates, and token average strategies are also presented. Results show that TS2-Net's performance rivals that of models with similar capacity to Longformer, while using significantly fewer parameters. Notably, TS2-Net's performance surpasses that of other efficient models like LLFA and LLSTM by a margin of 2-5%. This highlights the model's potential to effectively address the problem of retrieving and understanding long and complex video sequences. We believe that TS2-Net's innovative approaches to token representation and attention matrices can contribute to the advancement of future work in text-video retrieval and related areas. We also identify potential avenues for further improvement, such as adapting the model to process multiple modalities, such as audio and 3D video, and developing more efficient token representation and attention matrix pruning strategies. We hope that TS2-Net's techniques and results will inspire researchers to explore new possibilities in this area. Ultimately, we envision that TS2-Net's breakthroughs will lead to the development of more sophisticated and accurate models in the field of text-video retrieval and retrieval. We plan to continue working on this topic and look forward to contributing to the advancement of state-of-the-art techniques in the future. Within this framework, a flavour-altering neutral current (FANc) manifests as a purely flavour-changing neutral interaction involving the top quark's d- and s-quarks. Our analysis, primarily focused on flavour-changing neutral currents involving the d-quark, reveals that FANc's impact on top quark decays to a W boson, d quark, and an additional particle (which can be a quark or a leptonic particle) is minimal due to suppressed branching ratios. However, top quark decays to a W boson, d quark, and a leptonic particle with a muon or tau lepton significantly differ in their decay patterns from the standard model. Crucially, these FANc-induced top quark decay modes are expected to be detectable with a large number of events, even with the current large hadron collider (LHC) dataset. Our proposed observation methods for these FANc-induced top quark decay modes involve multiple variables and are classified into two categories. Method one involves the observation of FANc by examining top quark decay distributions in conjunction with a specific type of decay products containing a muon or tau lepton. Method two involves the observation of FANc by examining top quark decay distributions in two distinct sets of decay products and then combining them to identify FANc-induced signals. Our study shows that future LHC datasets with 300 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton collisions can potentially detect FANc-induced signals at a statistically significant level. Moreover, we have established upper limits on two types of couplings associated with FANc at a 95% confidence level. These limits are consistent with existing constraints on flavour-changing neutral interactions involving the d-quark and set more stringent constraints on flavour-changing neutral interactions involving the s-quark. Finally, we highlight the potential of a future proton-proton collider operating at 100 TeV to detect FANc-induced signals at a statistically significant level. Muons are a strong contender for the next generation of particle colliders due to their easy production in pairs, natural abundance, and low background rates. However, their use in collider form is hindered by beam-induced backgrounds resulting from their decay products, which pose a significant problem. Studies have revealed that these backgrounds could be detrimental to the sensitivity of future lepton colliders, potentially limiting them to an energy threshold of 1 TeV unless they find a way to mitigate these effects. This report provides an overview of potential strategies to combat beam-induced noise, including optimizing muon production, matching the muon acceleration rate with decay times, matching the beam energies, and using electron beams as proxies for muons. These studies, which have been conducted across a range of collider designs, suggest it's feasible to reduce Beam Induced Background by an order of magnitude, and further research is exploring the potential for an additional 10-fold reduction. This progress holds great promise for enabling muon colliders to meet their full potential in sensitivity. This chapter highlights the significance of geostatistics and machine learning in understanding atmospheric processes and their impact on public health. Traditional air pollution studies often rely on point-of-care measurements, but have been limited by a lack of understanding of atmospheric contamination models. Recent advancements have improved modeling capabilities, now incorporating atmospheric transport models and machine learning techniques to analyze pollution data. We introduce an innovative technique to address the issue of domain disparity in speech recognition using semi-supervised Inter-domain penalty. The Inter-domain penalty approach belongs to unsupervised domain adaptation methods that aim to reduce the effect of domain disparity. Unlike other methods that rely on similar layer representations across domains, Inter-domain penalty does not require pre-existing information about the target domain and can learn the importance of each feature on the fly. However, existing implementations of Inter-domain penalty only differed in their loss functions and used the same set of features to compute the penalty. This study presents a new implementation of Inter-domain penalty using cyclic consistency constraints based on Inter-domain penalty, which is referred to as Inter-domain penalty cycle (IIPC). The IIPC cycle can be viewed as a combination of two interconnected operations that improve the similarity of representations between domains. An active inference framework, rooted in brain theory, helps a low-cost robot 2 navigate and explore an unfamiliar environment (fig. 1).  With limited sensory and motor capabilities, the robot relies on independent decision-making to reach new locations and gather visual data (e.g., to identify a straight line) through trial and error.  By adopting a simplified brain model with hierarchical layers, the robot allocates computational resources to various tasks, prioritizing navigation over sensory exploration (sec. 2).  To enhance stability and accuracy in uncertain conditions, we developed an active inference method that encourages the robot to seek out consistent and predictable observations relevant to its goals (sec. 3).  Experimental results demonstrate that our approach leads to efficient and goal-oriented navigation while exploring the environment, outperforming comparable methods based on reinforcement learning (fig. 7).  Furthermore, we evaluated the robot's ability to adapt to changes in the environment and found that our approach is effective in a variety of goal-oriented and open-ended scenarios (sec. 4 and fig. 8).  In contrast, reinforcement learning methods often struggle to handle these types of challenges, requiring separate reward functions for each scenario.  Additionally, our approach provides a clear understanding of the robot's decision-making process, as it is grounded in a simplified model of the brain (sec. 5).  In summary, our research demonstrates that active inference is a valuable tool for developing goal-oriented and open-ended systems of intelligence (sec. 6). Our proposed system, Box Re-Ranking (BRR), effectively reduces false positives in pedestrian detection and is specifically designed to work with domain-adaptive pedestrian detection. BRR leverages object detection box data by employing a supervised neural network that incorporates a soft binning activation function. Unlike other approaches that rely on complex post-processing techniques or external training data, BRR operates entirely within a domain-adaptive pedestrian detection framework. By introducing box activation, over-Confident and distant negative boxes are repelled from the positive class, resulting in an improved false positive rate without compromising true positive detection rates. BRR does not require additional training or external ground truth and is compatible with existing pedestrian detection systems. When tested on the Citypersons dataset, BRR demonstrated a 53.6% reduction in false positives while increasing detection rates by 0.6%, outperforming a strong baseline by 7.9 mAP%. Furthermore, BRR was shown to be stable across a range of its hyperparameters and produced consistent results with minimal decline in detection rates when applied to the Caltech KITTI dataset and the Citypersons dataset. BRR was successfully integrated with the widely-used DeepSORT tracker, resulting in a significant 46% reduction in false positives while increasing detection rates by 0.6%, resulting in a 7.9% improvement in the mean average precision. When tested on the challenging Traffic4D dataset, BRR achieved the highest performance among all evaluated systems, resulting in a 11% increase in the mean average precision over the strongest baseline. BRR was also successfully applied to the traffic surveillance system of the University of Michigan's airfield, reducing false positives by 28% and increasing detection rates by 2%, resulting in a 10% improvement in the mean average precision. To effectively translate and parse human language, it is crucial to utilize the syntactic dependencies derived from tree structures. Prior studies have employed tree structured decoding methods within neural machine translation (NMT) frameworks, but these attempts have been hindered by inaccuracies in parsing and translation due to a lack of control over decoding direction. In contrast, existing tree parsing models are unable to directly leverage syntactic dependencies during the translation process. In order to overcome these limitations, this research introduces a novel tree structured decoding method that utilizes a syntax aware neural model to achieve simultaneous translation and parsing. Our approach begins by parsing an input sentence to generate a syntactically accurate tree structure, which is then utilized to derive multiple translation hypotheses based on the tree's branch and leaf properties. Our model achieves this process through a stack-based mechanism incorporating a set of rules. Our empirical evaluations demonstrate that the proposed model yields superior results in terms of both translation and parsing performance, which is supported by analysis of both objective and subjective translation outputs. Furthermore, our model outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in translation tasks involving multiple languages, including English to German and English to Russian, which are often characterized by irregularities in parsing and translation. This research presents a pioneering study on zero-shot voice translation without language supervision. A unique, end-to-end deep learning framework is designed to learn speech representations from two languages, utilizing the MuST-c dataset and a combination of residual connections to compensate for biased speech representations. We experiment with various connection configurations and show that our proposed approach can achieve state-of-the-art results on the English-Spanish and Spanish-English voice translation tasks across all metric scores. Notably, our model performs within 2.17 and 2.35 residual steps to reach the state-of-the-art, setting a new benchmark for zero-shot voice translation. Further, we successfully apply our model to translate speech between English and Portuguese, demonstrating its versatility across language pairs. Our full implementation is available online.

The accurate detection and quantification of COVID-19 pulmonary lesions in chest CT scans play a vital role in confirming diagnosis, treatment, and infection tracking. However, conventional fully-supervised lesion localization and segmentation methods rely on extensive, labor-intensive annotations, which can be time-consuming and costly to obtain, particularly in fields like medicine. To address this issue, we introduce a unique framework for lesion localization and segmentation that leverages weakly labeled data, including image-level labels only. This approach allows for the generation of lesion masks associated with specific images without requiring individual pixel annotations. We evaluate our approach on two well-known medical datasets and compare its performance to state-of-the-art fully-supervised methods using comprehensive quantitative and qualitative assessments. The results demonstrate that our approach yields comparable performance while significantly reducing the need for expensive pixel-level annotations. Additionally, when combined with additional multi-task training, our approach exhibits improved robustness to variations in data quality and adverse effects of class imbalance. To facilitate reproducibility, we open-source our approach on GitHub, along with the associated annotations and experimental results. In the fashion industry, searching for images based on fashion items is a common task, but due to the vast number of possible styles (e.g., T-shirt, skirt, dress), categorizing these items into garments is even more challenging. This problem is further complicated by the need for semantic manipulation of fashion items, where a query image showing a short sleeve may be transformed into an image with a long sleeve. This paper tackles these challenges through semi-supervised learning. First, we develop a feature-level representation of fashion items using a segmentation-free approach that extracts semantic features from unlabeled images. Next, we introduce a manipulation network to change a fashion item's core trait by initializing it with a mixture of semantic features. This allows us to set up a core feature for each fashion item and manipulate it without knowing the label. Finally, we integrate the feature-level representation and manipulation network into a retrieval framework, which enables us to select relevant fashion items based on a query image and manipulate its trait. Experiments on two datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in manipulating a fashion item's trait at the feature level.
